roles.description: Assist a preschool, elementary, middle, or secondary school teacher to provide academic, social, or life skills to students who have learning, emotional, or physical disabilities. Serve in a position for which a teacher has primary responsibility for the design and implementation of educational programs and services.
roles.sector: Educational instruction and library

tasks.label: Provide assistance to students with special needs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-class 1:1 or small-group academic support in a K-12 special education or inclusion classroom: sitting beside a student, re-explaining teacher directions, prompting and re-focusing, handing out and adapting worksheets and manipulatives, hand-over-hand writing guidance, scribing dictated answers, operating the student's AAC device, packing up materials.

Personal care and life-skills assistance for students with significant disabilities: escorting to the restroom and toileting/diapering and hygiene, hand-washing, dressing and undressing coats and shoes, mealtime feeding and drink assistance in the classroom or cafeteria, cleaning up spills and soiled clothing.

Physical assistance and mobility support: transferring a student between wheelchair, floor mat, stander and chair, repositioning and checking braces/orthotics, pushing a wheelchair or walking beside a student with a gait trainer between classroom, therapy room and bus loading zone, carrying out PT/OT-prescribed exercises.

Behavior support and 1:1 shadowing: monitoring an emotionally or behaviorally disabled student, reading early escalation signs, redirecting, delivering a token/reinforcement system, blocking self-injury or aggression, guiding the student to a de-escalation space, and physical crisis intervention when trained and necessary.

Assistance outside the classroom: supporting the student at recess/playground, in the cafeteria line, on field trips, on public transit, and during community-based instruction at a job site or grocery store, adapting to crowds, weather and unfamiliar layouts.

sources.title: Can Robots Help Autistic Children Better Their Academic Performance?
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo, the most widely used social robot in US special education classrooms, runs scripted social-emotional lessons while a human facilitator sits behind the student and selects the robot's responses on an iPad; it does not handle materials or provide physical assistance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-mediated social-skills instruction for students with autism in the same K-12 special education setting. It is the closest existing analogue to a paraprofessional's instructional support, and shows the robot is a facilitator-operated lesson-delivery tool rather than an autonomous aide.

sources.title: Salamanca, N.Y., Schools to Pilot AI Robot Teaching Assistant
sources.claim: The most advanced 2026 US classroom robot deployment, Realbotix's 'Sally' AI teaching assistant in Salamanca, NY, is a largely immobile conversational tutor for STEM camps and homework help; it performs no physical assistance to students.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: AI tutoring/teaching-assistant support in a K-12 classroom, the same setting as this task. It bounds what classroom robots do today: speech-based tutoring, with no manipulation of student materials, personal care, or mobility support.

sources.title: Robotic system feeds people with severe mobility limitations | Cornell Chronicle
sources.claim: Autonomous robot-assisted feeding of people with severe mobility limitations has been demonstrated only in small research studies, not deployed as a caregiving service.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assisted feeding of a person with a physical disability, one component of the personal-care instance. It shows the state of the art is a 13-participant study, short of the reliability an aide must deliver, and covers none of toileting, dressing or hygiene.

sources.title: Obi Robotic Feeding Device | School Health
sources.claim: Obi, the commercial robotic feeder sold to schools, requires a caregiver to set it up and requires the diner to trigger each bite with a switch and to chew and swallow unassisted, so it does not substitute for an aide feeding a student with complex needs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mealtime assistance for a student with a physical disability in a school. The device is user-commanded and caregiver-configured, so even the narrowest physical-care sub-step is not performed autonomously end-to-end.

sources.title: PTR Robots announces mobile robot for lifting and rehabilitating patients
sources.claim: Commercial person-lifting robots are caregiver-operated aids for transfers and gait training, not autonomous systems that move a person on their own.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: transferring and ambulating a dependent person, mechanically the same as wheelchair-to-stander transfers and gait-trainer walking for a student. The system augments a human operator rather than replacing one, so the instance cannot be completed autonomously.

sources.title: Teleop, not autonomy, is the path for 1X's Neo humanoid
sources.claim: General-purpose humanoids intended for unstructured human settings still rely on human teleoperators for complex whole tasks as of 2026.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: general mobile manipulation in human-occupied, cluttered settings, the capability any robot would need to shadow a student, physically assist, and manage materials. Teleoperation dependence means it cannot support a positive judgment.

tasks.label: Teach socially acceptable behavior, employing techniques such as behavior modification or positive reinforcement.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Supervise students in classrooms, halls, cafeterias, school yards, and gymnasiums, or on field trips.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Classroom supervision during instruction: a special-education TA monitors a small group or an assigned 1:1 student in a self-contained or inclusion classroom, scans for off-task, unsafe or self-injurious behavior, gives verbal and physical prompts, repositions students and equipment, blocks/redirects elopement or aggression, and implements behavior-intervention-plan responses (including trained physical escort or restraint) while the teacher instructs.

Hallway and transition supervision: escorting students between classroom, bathroom, therapy rooms and buses through crowded corridors and stairwells, keeping a wandering or runner student within bounds, pushing/steering a wheelchair or steadying an ambulatory student, managing peer conflicts and doorway congestion during passing periods.

Cafeteria supervision: seating and monitoring students at lunch, watching for choking, food allergies, food stealing or pica, providing feeding/utensil assistance and napkin/spill cleanup, prompting appropriate social behavior in a loud, crowded lunchroom, and de-escalating disputes.

School yard / recess supervision: outdoor playground duty in variable weather, tracking assigned students among many peers on climbing equipment and open blacktop, preventing wandering off grounds, spotting falls and injuries, mediating peer conflict, and physically assisting students with mobility or sensory needs.

Gymnasium / adaptive PE supervision: supporting students during PE or assemblies in a gym, guiding participation in games, spotting and physically assisting students with balance, mobility or coordination deficits, retrieving equipment, and providing a quiet-space break for a student who becomes dysregulated by noise.

Field trips and community-based instruction: supervising students off campus (bus loading, museum, park, grocery store, job site), maintaining constant line-of-sight and hand-holding or harness support in public crowds and near traffic, managing toileting, medication timing and behavioral crises in an unfamiliar, uncontrolled setting.

sources.title: Knightscope on X: What is the Knightscope K5 Autonomous Security Robot (ASR)?
sources.claim: Knightscope's K5 is a commercially deployed autonomous patrol robot marketed to school campuses; it performs route patrols, video/thermal monitoring and acts as a mobile call box, but it has no manipulators and cannot physically assist, prompt, escort or intervene with students.
sources.transferJustification: Closest related task is campus patrol/monitoring. It does not transfer: the K5 only observes and streams video on fixed outdoor routes, while supervising special-education students requires physical prompting, escorting, feeding/mobility assistance and behavioral intervention, none of which the K5 can perform.

sources.title: Helping learners with autism through innovative technology - LuxAI S.A.
sources.claim: QTrobot is a commercially sold social robot used in special-needs classrooms, but it is a tabletop/stationary interaction tool operated by a teacher, therapist or support worker during structured sessions rather than a system that supervises students in halls, cafeterias, yards or on trips.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is delivering social-skills lesson content to students with autism. It does not transfer to supervision: the robot is immobile, is run under adult supervision, and cannot monitor a moving group, intervene physically, or assume duty-of-care responsibility.

tasks.label: Provide students with disabilities with assistive devices, supportive technology, and assistance accessing facilities, such as restrooms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Restroom/toileting assistance in a school bathroom: escorting a student with physical or developmental disabilities, managing clothing fasteners, transferring the student on and off the toilet or a changing table, diapering or catheter/hygiene care, cleanup, handwashing, and documenting. Requires close physical contact, dignity, and infection control.

Providing and setting up supportive technology in the classroom: retrieving and charging a speech-generating AAC device or iPad, mounting it on the student's wheelchair tray or desk at the right angle, powering it up and loading the correct page set, attaching a switch or adapted keyboard, fitting an FM/hearing-assistance receiver, then prompting and troubleshooting during the lesson.

Providing and fitting adaptive physical equipment: slant boards, pencil grips, adapted scissors, weighted vest, seat cushion or wedge, AFO braces or splints, positioning the student in a stander/gait trainer, adjusting footrests and straps on a wheelchair to therapist specification.

Hands-on mobility and facility access support: walking a student with a gait belt or walker to therapy, the cafeteria, or the restroom, supervising stairs and doorways, transferring the student between wheelchair, floor mat, and classroom chair, and loading/unloading at the bus lift, with behavioral supervision throughout.

Transporting a student who can sit, board, and self-direct but cannot self-propel: pushing the manual wheelchair from the classroom to the library, cafeteria, therapy room, or restroom door along a familiar same-floor route in school corridors, then returning the chair.

Facility access outside the school building: field trips, community-based instruction, playground and recess, helping the student use ramps, curb cuts, uneven terrain, and unfamiliar public restrooms, with crowds, weather, and layouts that differ from site to site.

sources.system: WHILL Autonomous Drive System / WHILL Autonomous Model
sources.title: How Autonomous Wheelchairs Work | Aviation Pros
sources.claim: WHILL's Autonomous Drive System moves people with reduced mobility along pre-mapped indoor routes in airport terminals: the rider selects a destination on a touchscreen, the chair drives itself there with 360-degree obstacle detection and auto-stop, then self-returns to its dock.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: transporting a seated person with limited mobility to a destination inside a controlled facility. This is the same physical act as the aide's wheelchair-push escort within school corridors — comparable payload, speeds, indoor mapped routes and pedestrian traffic — so it transfers to the escort slice of 'assistance accessing facilities', though not to any hands-on transfer or personal-care step.

sources.developer: WHILL, Inc. with Envoy Air / American Airlines
sources.title: WHILL and Envoy Deploy Autonomous Service at U.S. Airports
sources.claim: The autonomous chairs are in commercial revenue service at multiple US and Japanese airports (LAX, MIA, DTW, Haneda, Narita, Kansai, Chubu), operated by airline ground handlers, with hundreds of thousands of completed passenger trips.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (moving a person with reduced mobility through an institutional facility); establishes deployment maturity and that an institution accepts the output in place of a human pusher for riders who need no hands-on help.

sources.title: Serve Robotics to Acquire Diligent Robotics, Expanding Physical AI Platform Beyond the Sidewalk
sources.claim: Moxi, an autonomous mobile manipulator, is deployed in over 25 US hospitals where it fetches and delivers supplies and specimens along corridors and uses its arm for pickups and drop-offs; its deployed work is item logistics between staff areas, not physical contact with patients.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous fetch-and-deliver of small items inside a structured human facility. It marks the frontier of deployed mobile manipulation in schools/hospital-like settings and shows the gap: no deployed capability for fitting, mounting, or adjusting equipment on a person.

sources.system: physically assistive robots (survey of the field, incl. Stretch, Jaco-based systems)
sources.developer: Nanavati, Ranganeni & Cakmak, University of Washington (Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems)
sources.title: Physically Assistive Robots: A Systematic Review of Mobile and Manipulator Robots That Physically Assist People with Disabilities
sources.claim: A 2024 systematic review of mobile and manipulator robots that physically assist people with disabilities in activities of daily living (ambulating, dressing, personal hygiene) finds the field is still research-stage, with end-to-end systems only recently becoming feasible and typically studied in small real-world trials.
sources.transferJustification: Directly covers the related tasks of robot-assisted hygiene, dressing, transfer and object handover to disabled people; establishes that these remain research demonstrations, frequently with shared/teleoperated control, rather than worker-quality autonomous care.

tasks.label: Carry out therapeutic regimens, such as behavior modification and personal development programs, under the supervision of special education instructors, psychologists, or speech-language pathologists.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Tutor and assist children individually or in small groups to help them master assignments and to reinforce learning concepts presented by teachers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Employ special educational strategies or techniques during instruction to improve the development of sensory- and perceptual-motor skills, language, cognition, or memory.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Self-contained elementary classroom: one-to-one systematic/discrete-trial instruction with a minimally verbal student with autism or intellectual disability — presenting picture cards and manipulatives, running a least-to-most prompt hierarchy including hand-over-hand physical guidance, delivering immediate reinforcement, taking trial data, and re-engaging the student after refusal or escalation.

Resource room: small-group multisensory language/literacy instruction following the teacher's plan (Orton-Gillingham style) — sand trays, letter tiles, sound cards, tapping out phonemes; physically correcting grip and letter formation, adjusting pacing and cueing per student's errors.

Inclusion general-education class: reinforcing cognition and memory strategies for a student with a learning disability — visual schedules, graphic organizers, chunking, mnemonic and repetition cues, re-explaining the teacher's content, prompting note-taking and fading support so the student works alongside peers.

Sensory room or gym: perceptual-motor and sensory-regulation activities on the student's sensory diet — setting up a balance/obstacle circuit, therapy ball, swing, weighted or deep-pressure input, sensory bins; physically spotting, guiding and safeguarding the child and judging when to return to class.

Preschool special-education room: play-based language and communication instruction on the floor — modeling PECS/AAC exchanges, physically positioning the child and materials, hand-over-hand for picture exchange, expanding utterances and prompting imitation during play.

Student with severe physical and multiple disabilities: positioning an adapted switch, eye-gaze board or AAC device and adapted materials, providing hand-over-hand switch activation and partial-participation prompting during the teacher's lesson.

sources.title: Robots For Autism Teach Human Emotion
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo humanoid is commercially deployed in hundreds of US/North American schools to deliver social-skills and phonics lesson modules to students with autism; it speaks and gestures but does not manipulate instructional materials or physically guide students.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered social-skills/phonics instruction to the same student population. Relevant because it is the closest deployed analogue of a special-education TA employing instructional strategies, but it covers only scripted verbal/screen content.

sources.title: How to run a lesson with your robot
sources.claim: A Milo lesson is run by a human facilitator on a tablet who connects the devices, selects the lesson, pauses it, records the cueing (prompting) delivered to the student, and applies calm-down tools when the student is about to melt down — i.e., the adult still employs the instructional and behavioral strategies.

sources.system: Social robots in education (NAO, Pepper, QTrobot and others, reviewed)
sources.title: Generative AI-powered social robots in education: opportunities and challenges from a Delphi study
sources.claim: Peer-reviewed review of social robots in education finds that robots used in empirical classroom studies have generally been teleoperated (Wizard-of-Oz) or autonomous only within narrow, pre-defined interaction and content boundaries.

sources.system: Kebbi (MOVIA Robotics) socially assistive robot instruction
sources.developer: MOVIA Robotics / Penn State researchers (Jürgensen & Kubina)
sources.title: Socially Assistive Robotic Instruction for Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder
sources.claim: In a US public elementary school, a small Kebbi socially assistive robot paired with a child tablet delivered instruction to three children with autism; the robot ran the session autonomously once started, but staff retained Wizard-of-Oz intervention and the robot handled no physical materials.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered one-to-one explicit instruction of a life skill in a school. Closest published evidence of autonomous instructional delivery to this student population; it is preliminary research with three children and no physical prompting or materials handling.

sources.title: TeachingBot: Robot Teacher for Human Handwriting
sources.claim: TeachingBot, a research robot arm, physically guides a human learner's hand along generated handwriting trajectories with variable impedance control, in a laboratory setting with cooperative adult learners.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: physical hand guidance for handwriting, the mechanical analogue of hand-over-hand prompting. It is a lab bench demonstration with cooperative adult learners gripping a fixed manipulator, not a child with disabilities being guided over classroom materials, so it does not transfer to the instructional instance.

sources.title: QTrobot for special needs education
sources.claim: LuxAI's QTrobot for special-needs education is sold to schools with pre-programmed curricula for emotional, social, language and cognitive skills; teachers choose and supervise the sessions and the robot delivers screen- and speech-based educational units without handling materials.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered social/communication/cognitive lesson units in special-needs classrooms — the same instructional targets named in this task, but limited to scripted verbal and tablet content under teacher supervision.

tasks.label: Enforce administration policies and rules governing students.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Observe students' performance, and record relevant data to assess progress.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Instruct and monitor students in the use and care of equipment and materials to prevent injuries and damage.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Self-contained or resource classroom academic activity: the TA shows students with learning/emotional disabilities how to hold and use scissors, glue, pencils, manipulatives and school-issued tablets/Chromebooks, circulates among 4-12 students while they work, verbally and physically redirects misuse (throwing, banging, chewing, yanking charging cords), and walks them through cleaning and putting materials away.

Life-skills / vocational training space (school kitchen, laundry, job-skills lab): TA demonstrates and supervises safe use and care of knives, toaster oven, microwave, blender, washer/dryer, cleaning chemicals and mops with one to four students with intellectual disabilities, using hand-over-hand prompting and standing ready to physically block or stop a burn, cut or spill.

Adaptive/assistive equipment: TA teaches an individual student to operate and care for a wheelchair, walker, gait trainer, stander, AAC speech device, hearing aids or adapted utensils - checking brakes and straps, correcting unsafe handling, teaching charging, cleaning and storage - and stays alongside to prevent falls or damage to costly devices.

Adapted PE, playground or sensory room: TA instructs a group in safe use of gym equipment, scooters, balls, climbing structures, swings, weighted vests and therapy balls, spots students, keeps a moving group in view, and intervenes physically to prevent collisions, falls and equipment misuse.

Preschool / early-childhood special education room: TA teaches 3-5 year olds with developmental delays to handle toys, books and sensory materials gently, to not mouth or throw small parts, and to help with cleanup; frequent physical redirection and immediate removal of hazards.

sources.title: Research and development | Kaspar the social robot | University of Hertfordshire
sources.claim: Kaspar, a child-sized social robot used in specialist autism schools, has run fully autonomous sessions prompting, encouraging and advising pairs of children during an imitation game - the closest demonstrated 'guide children with disabilities through an activity' capability, but limited to social prompts with no tool handling or safety intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: guiding children with autism through a structured activity in a special school. Transfer fails here: Kaspar is a seated, non-mobile humanoid that does not manipulate scissors, appliances or mobility equipment, does not scan a class for hazards, and cannot physically intervene to stop an injury or protect equipment.

sources.title: Surprising Performances of Students with Autism in Classroom with NAO Robot (arXiv:2407.12014)
sources.claim: NAO humanoid robots have been run inside real special-education school classrooms delivering group activities, but alongside special education teachers who conduct the class; the robot contributes speech and gesture, not equipment handling or safety supervision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: delivering instruction to students with disabilities in a special-education classroom (an E2 setting). It does not substantiate this task because the robot neither demonstrates use and care of physical equipment nor monitors and intervenes to prevent injury or damage.

sources.title: Autonomy in socially assistive robotics: a systematic review (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: A 2025 systematic review of socially assistive robotics finds the field still transitioning away from Wizard-of-Oz teleoperation, i.e. autonomous social-assistive behaviour with vulnerable users remains a research problem rather than a deployed capability.
sources.transferJustification: Field-level evidence on the autonomy of the robot class that would have to perform this task; establishes that autonomous supervision or coaching of people with disabilities is not an established deployed capability.

sources.system: physically assistive mobile and manipulator robots (survey)
sources.developer: Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems authors
sources.title: Physically Assistive Robots: A Systematic Review of Mobile and Manipulator Robots That Physically Assist People with Disabilities
sources.claim: A 2024 survey of physically assistive robots for people with disabilities characterises end-to-end systems interacting with disabled users in real settings as a growing research trend, not fielded practice; no product provides hands-on prompting and hazard intervention for schoolchildren.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robots physically assisting people with disabilities. Cited to show that the physical-assistance capability required by the hand-over-hand prompting and injury-prevention parts of this task is still at research stage.

sources.title: New York school district to pilot first humanoid robot teacher in US classroom (Audacy)
sources.claim: The most prominent 2026 US school humanoid deployment, Realbotix 'Sally' at Salamanca City Central School ..., is a stationary conversational robot that does not move about the classroom; students interact with it and its avatar on laptops.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: a robot acting as a classroom teaching assistant. It cannot substantiate this task: the robot is immobile and conversational, with no ability to handle materials, follow students, or intervene physically.

tasks.label: Present subject matter to students under the direction and guidance of teachers, using lectures, discussions, supervised role-playing methods, or by reading aloud.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Discuss assigned duties with classroom teachers to coordinate instructional efforts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Instruct students in daily living skills required for independent maintenance and self-sufficiency, such as hygiene, safety, or food preparation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: School restroom or classroom sink: teaching aide runs a task-analyzed hygiene routine (handwashing, toothbrushing, grooming, toileting) with a student with moderate-to-severe intellectual/physical disability — models each step, uses gestural then hand-over-hand physical prompting with prompt fading, manages resistance or sensory refusal, cleans up, and records trial-by-trial IEP data.

School life-skills kitchen: aide sets out ingredients and a picture recipe, models and prompts a student through making a snack or simple meal using a knife, toaster, microwave or stovetop, physically guards hot and sharp hazards and intervenes if the student acts unsafely, then guides washing up.

Classroom or resource room, higher-functioning students: aide reviews a visual checklist for grooming/hygiene/self-care, gives verbal reminders and contingent feedback while the student performs the routine independently, reinforces success, and records progress toward the goal — little or no physical contact needed.

School setting, safety instruction and rehearsal: fire/lockdown drill practice, kitchen and tool safety rules, medicine and stranger safety, simulated street crossing in a hallway or gym — role play with prompting, correction, and physically keeping students safe during practice.

Community-based instruction: aide accompanies one to three students to a grocery store, laundromat, restaurant or bus stop, prompts shopping, paying, ordering and street crossing among traffic and strangers, and keeps students safe throughout.

sources.title: Project ALMI pilots: assistive robots helping in the kitchen
sources.claim: PAL Robotics' TIAGo, in the ALMI project demonstrator, autonomously coached a user with mild motor and cognitive impairments through meal preparation with step-by-step voice instructions and handed over ingredients and utensils; it is a research demonstrator in a simulated domestic kitchen with a cooperative adult, without hazard intervention or assessment of skill acquisition.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: verbally coaching an impaired adult through meal preparation. Shares kitchen objects and setting with food-preparation instruction, but the recipient is a cooperative adult in a single demonstrator scenario; the robot does not physically prompt, guard hot or sharp hazards, manage behavior, or assess mastery, so it does not carry over to teaching a student with disabilities.

sources.title: QTrobot for special needs education - LuxAI S.A.
sources.claim: QTrobot, a leading commercial special-needs-education robot, ships with curricula that include autonomy/self-help units, but sessions are run by an adult: the package includes an educator tablet used to control the robot, and the robot is a seated tabletop platform that handles no materials.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered social, emotional and self-help lessons to students with disabilities — the closest commercial analogue to a special-education aide's instruction, showing that the robot remains educator-operated and cannot perform or supervise physical self-care routines.

sources.title: Milo Technical FAQ | Robots4Autism
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo is deployed in North American school districts for autism instruction, but each session requires a human facilitator running the lesson from a tablet beside the student, and the content is social-emotional rather than hygiene, safety or food-preparation routines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-mediated skill instruction for students with autism in schools. Shows the state of practice for classroom instruction robots — a human facilitator stays in the loop and the robot never handles materials or physical routines.

sources.developer: AMMACHI Labs, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham / University of Glasgow
sources.title: Enhancing Hand Hygiene Practices Through a Social Robot-Assisted Intervention in a Rural School in India
sources.claim: The WallBo social robot was pilot-deployed at a school handwashing station to promote hand hygiene among children and raised compliance, but it nudges and encourages rather than delivering individualized self-care instruction, and the pilot's autonomy is not established.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: prompting schoolchildren to wash their hands. Same setting type (school washbasin) and skill area (hygiene), but with typically developing children and only compliance nudging — no task-analytic teaching, physical prompting, individualization or IEP data collection.

sources.system: social robots deployed in K-12 classrooms (field-study review)
sources.title: The use of social robots in classrooms: A review of field-based studies
sources.claim: A review of field-based studies of social robots in real classrooms finds they are seldom run autonomously for more than a few days, indicating that unattended, sustained robot-delivered classroom instruction is not established practice.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered classroom instruction generally. Bounds the autonomy and reliability achievable by any robot standing in for a classroom aide.

sources.system: Optio / Realbotix M-Series humanoid teaching assistant
sources.developer: Realbotix (Salamanca City Central School District pilot)
sources.title: US Firm's Humanoid Robot Teaching Assistant to Support 500 Students in 2026
sources.claim: The newest humanoid classroom assistant reaching US schools is a conversational AI tutor for high-school coding and AI courses — a talking humanoid platform with no manipulation of materials and no role in self-care or life-skills routines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: a humanoid robot serving as a ... a school. Shows that even 2026-vintage school humanoids are conversational tutors for academic subjects, with no demonstrated hygiene, safety or cooking instruction.

tasks.label: Prepare classrooms with a variety of materials or resources for children to explore, manipulate, or use in learning activities or imaginative play.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Elementary or preschool special-education classroom, before school or between rotations: the aide lays out learning-center materials per the teacher's plan — counting bears, linking cubes, puzzles, sorting trays, leveled books, whiteboards and markers — across three to five tables/centers, arranging them so students with motor and attention needs can reach and use them, often while furniture, backpacks and a few early-arriving students are in the room.

Early-childhood / self-contained special-ed room: setting up sensory and imaginative-play areas — filling a sensory bin with rice, beans, water beads or water and burying small objects in it, arranging play-kitchen props, dolls, dress-up clothes and soft-play mats, putting out playdough and tools at a table.

Prep-table or workroom work making the consumables: printing, cutting and laminating picture symbols, then trimming and velcro-mounting them; assembling task boxes and individual student work folders; portioning art supplies (glue sticks, paint cups, scissors, paper) into per-student trays or caddies for the next activity.

Reset and restock after an activity: collecting scattered manipulatives, art materials, toys and game pieces from tables and floor, sorting them back into labeled bins on the correct shelves, wiping/sanitizing shared toys, and replenishing consumables from the classroom storage closet so the room is ready for the next group.

Secondary or life-skills special-ed setting: setting up functional/vocational task stations (kitchen items for a cooking lesson, laundry sorting, coin/money tasks, packaging job tasks) and staging individualized supports for named students — mounting an AAC device, positioning a slant board, weighted vest, adapted switch toy or communication board where the student can access it.

sources.title: Staples deploys RightHand Robotics tech in its fulfillment centers | Supply Chain Dive
sources.claim: RightHand Robotics' RightPick piece-picking arms are deployed across Staples' North American fulfillment centers, autonomously grasping items of widely varying shape, size and packaging and placing them into order containers inside a fenced robotic cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: order picking/kitting of assorted small consumer goods. Classroom-material prep at E1 reduces to picking assorted small items (crayons, blocks, puzzle pieces, books, glue sticks) from presented totes and placing them into designated trays or caddies — comparable object variety, comparable placement precision, same fixtured presentation.

sources.title: Amazon uses robots that sort, lift, and carry packages—see them in action
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm identifies and picks individual retail products from bins and places them into totes in fulfillment centers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: singulating and placing individual items into a designated container. Assembling per-student material sets at E1 is the same pick-and-place-into-designated-receptacle operation over a similar mix of small consumer items.

sources.title: AI Robotics for the Real World | Covariant
sources.claim: Covariant's AI-controlled pick-and-place robots are sold as handling essentially arbitrary warehouse SKUs in goods-to-robot cells, including small and oddly shaped items.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: general item handling in a fixtured picking cell. It substantiates that grasp variety — the main difficulty of handling a classroom's heterogeneous manipulatives and supplies — is solved when items are presented to the machine.

sources.title: Nimble picks up $106M to scale general purpose fulfillment robot - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Nimble's autonomous fulfillment robots handle apparel and other soft/deformable goods along with hard goods in its robotic fulfillment centers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: picking deformable soft goods. Dress-up clothes, plush toys and fabric play props are the deformable elements of play-area prep; apparel handling in a fixtured picking cell is the closest substantiated analogue.

sources.system: AMP ONE / AMP Cortex sortation robots
sources.title: AMP to Operate Waste Connections Recycling Facility with AI-Powered Sortation Technology
sources.claim: AMP's AI-guided sorting robots are deployed at scale in materials recovery facilities, autonomously identifying heterogeneous objects moving past on conveyors and diverting each into the correct category bin.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sorting a stream of mixed, previously unseen objects into category bins. Putting classroom materials away at E1 — items presented on a belt, sorted into the correct labeled bin — is the same recognize-and-divert operation at comparable object variety.

sources.title: Restocking robots deployed in 300 Japanese convenience stores - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Telexistence's TX SCARA robots restock beverage shelves in 300 FamilyMart convenience stores, running autonomously in normal operation with remote human takeover only to recover from dropped or misplaced items.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: placing stock items into defined shelf positions in a retail facility. It shows commercial-grade placement of uniform items in a rail-constrained, purpose-built work volume — supporting E1-style shelf loading, but not free-form arrangement of varied materials around a room.

sources.title: How Diligent's Robots Are Making a Difference in Texas Hospitals - IEEE Spectrum
sources.claim: Diligent's Moxi performs commercial autonomous mobile manipulation inside hospitals, retrieving supplies from supply closets and delivering them ....
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fetching and delivering supplies inside a structured institutional building (E2). It is the strongest deployed E2 mobile-manipulation case, but it is limited to grasping bagged/boxed supplies and transporting them; it does not substantiate laying out varied materials across classroom work stations.

sources.title: Figure's Humanoid Robot Picks Up Toys, Wipes Surfaces in New Demo | eWeek
sources.claim: Figure showed its Helix 02 humanoid autonomously tidying a staged living room end to end — picking up toys, sorting objects and wiping surfaces — under a single learned policy.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: whole-room object pick-up and put-away, the closest analogue to classroom reset. It is a curated vendor demo in a staged room with no reported success rate, throughput or deployment, so it does not establish worker-quality completion in a real classroom.

sources.title: A VLA with Open-World Generalization
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's π0.5 policy drives a mobile manipulator to clean ... homes never seen in training, though the developers state it makes frequent mistakes.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: tidying/arranging everyday objects in unseen rooms. It is research-grade with self-reported frequent semantic and physical errors, so it shows partial capability in unstructured rooms but not worker-quality completion of classroom setup.

sources.system: Duplo DC-618 slitter/cutter/creaser and DFL-700 laminator
sources.title: Duplo Print Finishing Solutions Presented by GBC
sources.claim: Duplo's automated print-finishing systems slit, cut, crease and laminate printed sheets in a single automated pass in commercial print shops.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: cutting and laminating printed sheets. Making picture-symbol cards, labels and task-box printables is the same print-finishing operation, done on fixtured sheet-fed machines rather than by hand with a laminator and scissors.

sources.system: All-Fill auger and vibratory weigh fillers
sources.title: Granules & Granular Product Packaging Machines | All-Fill Inc.
sources.claim: All-Fill's auger and vibratory weigh fillers automatically dispense measured quantities of granular media into containers on packaging lines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: metered filling of containers with granular material. Filling a sensory bin with rice, beans or beads at E1 is the same dispensing operation with the bin presented in a fixed position under the filler.

tasks.label: Distribute teaching materials, such as textbooks, workbooks, papers, and pencils, to students.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Self-contained elementary special education classroom: TA hands out differentiated worksheets, workbooks and pencils/adapted grips to 6-10 students seated at small-group tables; each student gets a different version per their IEP, some need the sheet placed and oriented in front of them with a verbal prompt.

Inclusion / general-education classroom: TA passes out papers, tests, textbooks or manipulatives down rows of 20-30 desks (often starting stacks at the head of each row), while stepping around backpacks, chairs and students moving between activities.

Preschool / early-childhood special education room: TA distributes crayons, glue sticks, paper and manipulatives to 3-5 year olds at low tables or seated on a carpet; children reach, grab, drop and wander, and materials must be given one at a time to control behavior.

Secondary resource room or life-skills class: TA distributes textbooks, workbooks, calculators, laptops/tablets and assignment packets from a cart or supply shelf to students at tables, matching device/packet numbers to students and collecting them at the end.

Individual delivery to a student with significant physical disabilities: TA positions the worksheet/communication board on a wheelchair tray or slant board and places the pencil or adapted tool into the student's hand, sometimes with hand-over-hand support.

sources.title: Amazon robotics: Meet the robots inside fulfillment centers
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm autonomously identifies and picks individual, varied items out of containers and places them into the tote belonging to a specific customer order, in production fulfillment centers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: order picking. Selecting the correct item for a named recipient from bulk supply and placing it in that recipient's set is the sorting core of handing each student their own materials; objects (books, boxed pencils, packets) are comparable, and the cell is purpose-built.

sources.title: Galbot brings in $300M to scale mobile manipulator deployments - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Galbot's G1 mobile manipulator runs fully autonomous retail stores where the robot retrieves requested products from shelves and delivers them to the customer at the store window; stores operate in over 30 Chinese cities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: unmanned retail fulfillment. Fetching a named item and presenting it to the person who requested it, at a station built around the robot, is the hand-out step of distributing materials; item sizes (snacks, boxes, medicine cartons) match workbooks and pencil boxes.

sources.system: ScriptPro Robotic Prescription Dispensing System (SP Central)
sources.title: SCRIPTPRO ROBOTIC PRESCRIPTION DISPENSING SYSTEMS (brochure)
sources.claim: ScriptPro robotic prescription dispensing systems automatically select, fill and label patient-specific prescriptions inside a purpose-built pharmacy cell, with collating control centers that organize output by patient; installed in thousands of pharmacies.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: per-patient dispensing. Assembling and collating individually assigned items for named people at high accuracy in a machine-built cell transfers to assembling per-student material sets for pickup; the error tolerance there is stricter than a classroom's.

sources.system: BlueCrest / Pitney Bowes Mailstream Evolution inserter
sources.title: Bluecrest aka Pitney Bowes "MSE" Mailstream Evolution Inserter, 14F | EP Solutions
sources.claim: Production mail inserters in daily commercial use feed single sheets from high-capacity stacks, accumulate them into per-recipient sets verified by barcode cameras, fold and insert them.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: document set assembly. Separating and collating single sheets of paper into named recipients' sets is the hardest material-handling element of handing out worksheets; these machines do it in fixtured feed paths at production rates.

sources.title: Obi 3 Robotic Feeding Device – Adaptive Mealtime Independence
sources.claim: The Obi robotic feeding device is a commercial assistive robot used in homes, schools and therapy centers: a taught robotic arm picks portions from four fixed compartments and presents them precisely to a seated user with limited upper-body mobility, triggered by the user's accessibility switch.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assistive feeding. Presenting an item accurately to a specific seated student with a physical disability, from fixtured supply at a calibrated station, is the same delivery geometry as placing a material within that student's reach.

sources.title: Swisslog Healthcare Partners with Diligent Robotics to Enhance Hospital Logistics
sources.claim: Diligent Robotics' Moxi mobile robot autonomously delivers supplies, labs and medications point-to-point in more than 25 US ..., using its arm for doors and elevators while staff load and unload its compartments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: intra-facility supply delivery in a structured human facility (E2). It marks the demonstrated ceiling: payload transport between locations with humans loading and unloading, not per-person placement of individual items.

sources.title: Bear Robotics Servi — Price, Specs & Demo | RobotLAB
sources.claim: Bear Robotics' Servi autonomously runs trays of food to guest tables in restaurants; diners or staff take the items off the tray and the robot performs no manipulation of individual items.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: delivering items to seated people in a crowded human facility. Shows navigation among seated people is solved, but the give-the-right-item-to-the-right-person step is still done by humans.

sources.title: Naver's 1784 building showcases human-robot interaction - The Korea Times
sources.claim: Naver Labs operates about 110 Rookie service robots that autonomously deliver coffee, lunch boxes, documents and parcels to individual employees inside the 1784 office building.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: personalized item delivery to people at desks in an institutional building. Nearest analogue to classroom distribution, but the recipient retrieves the item from a compartment; the robot does not select, place or hand over materials.

sources.title: π0.5: a VLA with Open-World Generalization
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's pi-0.5 vision-language-action model lets a mobile bimanual robot perform household manipulation in homes not seen in training, but the developers state it is far from perfect ... frequently errs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: open-world mobile manipulation. It is the strongest generalist manipulation result in unstructured, people-occupied rooms and is explicitly error-prone, so it cannot support worker-quality distribution in an occupied classroom.

tasks.label: Organize and supervise games and other recreational activities to promote physical, mental, and social development.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Recess/playground duty at an elementary or middle school: the paraeducator takes an assigned group (including students with autism, ADHD, or physical disabilities) outdoors, sets out balls/jump ropes, starts and referees inclusive games, keeps students within boundaries, scans for unsafe play, breaks up conflicts, physically steadies or assists a student on climbing equipment or a wheelchair user on uneven blacktop, and responds to falls and injuries.

Adapted physical education / motor-group session in a school gym or multipurpose room: sets out cones, mats, scooters, parachute or bowling ramp; explains and modifies a group game (relay, target toss, movement circuit) for varied ability levels; demonstrates; provides hand-over-hand assistance, spotting, wheelchair pushing and physical prompting; watches for seizures, elopement, or over-exertion; puts equipment away.

One-on-one structured play/social-skills session with a single student at a table in a self-contained classroom or therapy room: turn-taking games, matching/board/card games, imitation and joint-attention play, reinforcement and data collection on responses, prompting and redirection, then clean-up.

Small-group table or floor game with 2-6 students with disabilities (indoor recess, board games, cooperative games, social-skills game groups): distributes pieces, explains and enforces rules, cues turn-taking and sharing, mediates disputes, manages behavior escalations, and keeps all students engaged and safe.

Preschool / early-childhood special education free-play and sensory-motor centers: sets up play stations (blocks, sand/water table, ball pit, obstacle course, music-and-movement), gets down on the floor to model and join play, rotates children, redirects unsafe behavior (mouthing, climbing, hitting), toilets/handles messes, and leads clean-up.

Off-campus or after-school recreation: escorting students to a park, bowling alley, community center, Special Olympics practice or school dance; organizing the activity in a space the school does not control, watching for wandering, assisting with mobility and equipment, and managing interactions with the public.

sources.system: DREAM robot-enhanced therapy system (NAO + multi-camera/depth sensing rig)
sources.developer: DREAM consortium (Babes-Bolyai University, University of Skovde, Plymouth, Portsmouth, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, SoftBank Robotics)
sources.title: Robot-enhanced therapy: development and validation of a supervised autonomous robotic system for autism spectrum disorders therapy (IEEE RAM), University of Portsmouth research portal
sources.claim: The DREAM project built a supervised-autonomous NAO-based robot-enhanced therapy (RET) system that runs structured imitation, joint-attention and turn-taking activities with children with ASD in an instrumented clinic therapy room, with robot control going beyond Wizard-of-Oz teleoperation; clinical results reported performance equivalent to standard human therapy.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered turn-taking/imitation play sessions with a child with autism. It transfers to the teaching assistant's one-on-one structured game session because it is the same population, the same tabletop game-like activities aimed at social development, in the same kind of indoor room, and the outcome measure (child's turn-taking/social skill performance) is the accepted output.

sources.title: The Efficacy of Robot-enhanced Therapy for Children With Autism Spectrum Disorders (NCT03323931), ClinicalTrials.gov
sources.claim: Randomized trial registration describes the intervention arm as an ABA-derived treatment delivered by a semi-autonomous robotic ... over 8 biweekly 45-minute sessions while a therapist supervises the session.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: the robot leads structured turn-taking/joint-attention play with one child; the therapist's role is supervisory rather than step-by-step control, matching the 'limited intervention' allowance.

sources.title: Efficacy and effectiveness of robot-assisted therapy for autism spectrum disorder: From lab to reality, Science Robotics
sources.claim: Peer-reviewed trials report that in-clinic robot-assisted therapy targeting joint attention, imitation and turn-taking achieved outcomes equivalent to conventional therapy with higher child engagement (n=69), and a second trial with simplified systems intended for schools and homes (n=63) also matched standard treatment.
sources.transferJustification: Corroborates worker-quality outcomes for robot-led turn-taking/imitation play sessions with young children with autism; autonomy level is not stated in the retrieved text, so it is treated as supporting context only.

sources.title: DREAM Lite: Simplifying Robot Assisted Therapy for ASD (arXiv:2104.08034)
sources.claim: The simplified version of the DREAM protocols that was actually deployed in ordinary educational centres removed the external sensor rig, which greatly reduced the robot's decision-making, and relies on a therapist driving the session from a tablet interface.
sources.transferJustification: Directly relevant negative evidence: in an ordinary school/clinic room (E2 conditions) the same activity is delivered under continuous therapist tablet control, so E2 autonomy is not substantiated.

sources.title: RoboKind Changes the Lives of Students on the Autism Spectrum Nationwide, Tech & Learning
sources.claim: Milo is a commercially deployed social robot used in hundreds of US school districts to deliver social-emotional lessons to students with autism, in facilitator-run weekly or biweekly sessions.
sources.transferJustification: Shows what is actually fielded in US special-education classrooms: a facilitator-operated curriculum robot for one student at a time, not an autonomous supervisor of games; autonomy is not established, so it cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.title: QTrobot for special needs education - LuxAI S.A.
sources.claim: QTrobot is sold commercially to special-needs schools and therapy centres as an assistive tool operated by a teacher, therapist or parent, delivering pre-built educational units to a child.
sources.transferJustification: Fielded special-education robot, but it is an adult-operated tool used alongside the staff member rather than a system that organizes and supervises an activity on its own; autonomy unclear.

sources.system: NAO robotic exercise coach with Kinect tracking
sources.title: Robotic System for Physical Training of Older Adults, International Journal of Social Robotics
sources.claim: A NAO humanoid paired with a Kinect was programmed as a robotic coach that instructs users through exercise routines and tracks their performance, demonstrated with older adults.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led physical activity instruction. It covers only verbal/gestural instruction to a single cooperative adult in a lab; it does not cover equipment setup, hands-on physical assistance, spotting, or group safety supervision for children with disabilities, so it does not carry over to the adapted-PE instance.

tasks.label: Use computers, audio-visual aids, and other equipment and materials to supplement presentations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Whole-class or small-group lesson support in a special education classroom: at the teacher's direction, run the classroom computer, projector or interactive panel — cue up and play a video or slide deck, advance slides on cue, turn on captions, adjust volume, switch to a document camera — while the teacher presents to students with learning, emotional or physical disabilities.

Distribute and set up student devices for a lesson: pull Chromebooks/tablets and headphones from the charging cart, hand them to each student at their seat, help students log in and open the correct app or e-book, fit headphones and adjust positioning for students with motor or sensory needs, then collect and re-dock the devices.

Prepare supplementary teaching materials in the classroom workroom or prep area: print, cut and laminate picture cards, visual schedules and adapted worksheets; assemble manipulative kits and task boxes; sort them into per-student sets ready for the upcoming presentation.

One-to-one assistive technology support during instruction: mount and position an AAC speech device, switch or eye-gaze unit on a student's wheelchair tray or desk, calibrate it, provide hand-over-hand or physical prompting on the touchscreen/switch as the teacher presents, and reposition or re-attach the equipment when the student moves.

Set up, connect and troubleshoot AV equipment: wheel the AV cart to the classroom or resource room, connect a laptop via HDMI/USB-C adapter and audio cable, power up the projector or panel, pair a Bluetooth speaker or FM/hearing-assist transmitter, and fix a 'no signal', sound or battery problem so the presentation can start on time.

sources.title: Social robots for education: a global analysis of deployments in real scenarios
sources.claim: The Milo humanoid robot (RoboKind) is deployed in real North American school special-education programs, where it delivers instructional content to autistic students.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered instruction to special-education students. It transfers to 'use computers and audio-visual aids to supplement presentations' because the robot supplies the audio-visual instructional content to the same students in the same classroom setting.

sources.title: IESD Case Study: Children on the Autism Spectrum Show Improvement with Robots4Autism
sources.claim: Milo delivers curriculum lessons verbally while driving a linked student tablet that shows multiple-choice options, text, images and video modeling — a machine running the audio-visual side of a lesson for students with disabilities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-run multimedia lesson delivery. Same media objects (tablet content, video, images), same students and same classroom; the AV-supplement function of the instance is exactly what the robot performs.

sources.title: The School District of Manatee County Becomes First in Florida to Adopt RoboKind's Robot and Social-Emotional Curriculum for Students with Autism
sources.claim: A US school district adopted RoboKind's robot program district-wide; students in groups or one-on-one receive lessons from the robot with on-body symbol displays and tablet video.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led delivery of AV lesson content in a school classroom; transfers because the physical demand (presenting media to seated students) and the environment are the same as in the instance.

sources.title: QTrobot for special needs education - LuxAI S.A.
sources.claim: QTrobot is a commercial special-needs education robot supplied to schools with hundreds of pre-built educational units that it runs with students.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot presenting structured educational content to special-needs students in school settings; corroborates that machines already fill the AV-presentation role in this exact environment.

sources.system: Danfoss Drives kitting cell with Roboception 3D stereo vision
sources.title: Case Studies: Automated Kitting Solution with 3D Robot Vision
sources.claim: A production kitting cell autonomously picks assorted parts from supplier pallets with 3D vision and assembles them into trays — the industrial analogue of assembling per-student material kits in a fixtured cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic kitting. Transfers to preparing per-student material sets because it is the same operation — vision-guided picking of assorted small items into labelled trays — inside a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: FANUC CRX collaborative robot (Athena automated production system)
sources.title: FANUC CRX Cobots for Machine Tending & Part Transfer
sources.claim: FANUC CRX collaborative robots are commercially deployed for machine tending and part transfer, e.g. an automated production system that doubled part output and raised machine utilization.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine tending. Feeding sheets or cards into a laminator or cutter and unloading them is the same load/unload cycle on a fixtured machine that cobots run in production today.

sources.system: Dynamic Compliance Tuning sim-to-real insertion policy on an industrial arm
sources.title: Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap with Dynamic Compliance Tuning for Industrial Insertion
sources.claim: Learned force-controlled policies perform autonomous industrial connector insertion at high reliability on a fixtured workpiece.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: connector insertion. AV hookup is largely mating display/audio/network-class plugs; objects and precision are comparable, with the socket fixtured in a cell.

sources.title: RLDG: Robotic Generalist Policy Distillation via Reinforcement Learning
sources.claim: A reinforcement-learning-distilled policy on a fixtured table performs autonomous insertion of exactly the connector families used in AV setup, including HDMI and DisplayPort.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: cable/connector mating into a fixed socket. Same connector types as classroom AV hookup (HDMI, USB-C, audio), demonstrated with the port fixtured to the table.

sources.title: Swisslog Healthcare Partners with Diligent Robotics to Enhance Hospital Logistics
sources.claim: Moxi mobile manipulators autonomously fetch and deliver supplies inside hospitals at scale, showing autonomous material transport within a structured human facility.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous point-to-point supply delivery in an institutional building. It covers only the transport leg of device/material handling; it does not hand items to seated individuals or set them up for them.

tasks.label: Clean classrooms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: After snack, lunch, art, or sensory activities, the TA wipes and sanitizes student tables, individual desks, work-station trays, and high-touch surfaces (door handles, switches, adaptive equipment), removing crumbs, spilled milk, paint, glue and drool, first pushing aside papers, crayons and manipulatives left on the surfaces; classroom is a standard school room, often with students still present.

End-of-session/end-of-day floor care of the classroom: sweeping or vacuuming the carpet and rug area and dust-mopping the tile, after chairs are pushed in or up, to remove crumbs, paper scraps, sand and glitter accumulated during the day.

Mid-activity spot cleanup of a localized floor mess while class is in session: a knocked-over cup of paint water, spilled juice, dumped sensory bin of rice or sand, crushed crackers under a table, requiring paper towels, a hand broom and dustpan, and a disinfectant mop in a small area among seated students and equipment.

Tidying and putting materials away: returning toys, blocks, puzzle pieces, communication cards, books, and art supplies to labeled bins and shelves, straightening desks and stacking chairs, organizing the reading corner and sensory area at transitions or end of day.

Cleaning up after a bodily-fluid or feeding accident involving a student with disabilities: toileting accident, vomit, or spilled tube-feed/food, cleaning and changing the student, bagging soiled clothing, and disinfecting the floor, chair, wheelchair or mat, following bloodborne-pathogen procedures.

Cleaning the classroom's life-skills kitchenette and utility areas: washing and drying dishes, cups and utensils used in cooking/feeding lessons, scrubbing the sink and counter, emptying trash bins into liners, and restocking soap, towels and gloves.

sources.system: Tennant T380AMR / X4 ROVR with BrainOS
sources.title: Denver Public Schools Leverages Robotic Floor Scrubbers to Meet Cleaning and Labor Challenges [Case Study]
sources.claim: BrainOS-powered Tennant robotic floor scrubbers are deployed at scale by a large US school district to autonomously scrub school floors, i.e. routine floor care inside school buildings.

sources.title: Five New Technologies in Education Transforming School Operations

tasks.label: Organize and label materials and display students' work in a manner appropriate for their eye levels and perceptual skills.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-lesson/end-of-day organizing in a self-contained special education classroom: gathering mixed manipulatives, art supplies, books, task-box pieces and adaptive tools left on tables and the floor, sorting them by category and returning them to the correct labeled bins, tubs and shelf positions so students can find them independently.

Creating and affixing labels: printing or writing picture-symbol plus word labels, laminating and cutting them, and sticking/velcroing them onto storage bins, tubs, cubbies, folders, drawers and desks so materials are identifiable by non-readers.

Mounting and refreshing a display of students' work on a classroom bulletin board or hallway board: trimming/backing papers, arranging them with a header at the students' standing eye level, and stapling or taping them to the board without damaging the work.

Making, mounting and updating individual visual supports: assembling velcro picture schedules, first-then boards, choice boards and token strips, and posting them on walls, desks or student binders at each child's eye level, then swapping cards as the day progresses.

Adapting materials and displays for one student's perceptual needs: enlarged high-contrast or tactile/braille labels, uncluttered spacing, and placing labels and displayed work at wheelchair or floor-sitting eye height for that student.

sources.title: Amazon introduces Sparrow—a state-of-the-art robot that handles millions of diverse products

sources.transferJustification: Related task: item-level picking and sortation of heterogeneous small goods into destination containers. It transfers to sorting mixed classroom materials into labeled bins because the objects (small consumer-goods-sized items) and the required precision are comparable, provided the items are presented to the machine as a purpose-built cell would present them.

instances.label: In the school workroom/copy room: printing and photocopying worksheets, adapted/enlarged-print packets and homework sheets for individual IEPs, collating multi-page sets, stapling or binding them, and sorting into per-student folders or bins. Mixed paper sizes and jams, several jobs at once, needed before the next period.

Making visual supports and manipulatives: printing picture-symbol cards, visual schedules, token boards and matching/sorting sets; cutting them apart with scissors or a paper trimmer, running them through a pouch/roll laminator, trimming again, sticking on Velcro dots, and sorting the pieces into labeled envelopes, folders or task boxes.

Creating and mounting a bulletin board or classroom display: covering the board with butcher paper, stapling on a border, cutting or arranging letters, and stapling/pinning student work and visual anchors in the layout the teacher specified, on a wall in the classroom or hallway, often from a step stool between classes.

Setting up and checking equipment for the day's lessons: charging and staging AAC devices, tablets and headphones, loading the right communication board or app, connecting and testing the projector/interactive display, mounting a switch on a wheelchair tray, positioning adaptive seating, slant boards or sensory equipment.

Setting up a hands-on demonstration or activity stations: portioning art supplies, science demo items, or cooking/life-skills ingredients and utensils into individual trays or station kits and placing them at each student's work area, with adaptations (pre-cut pieces, non-spill containers) for particular students.

tasks.label: Assist in bus loading and unloading.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Afternoon dismissal at the school bus loading zone: the TA walks a small group of ambulatory students with disabilities (autism, intellectual disability, ADHD) from the classroom to the curb, holds hands or uses proximity prompts to keep them out of the driveway lane, matches each student to the correct bus, hands off notes/communication logs to the driver or monitor, and watches until doors close. Outdoors, all weather, dozens of buses and other students moving.

Morning arrival unloading at the school entrance: TA meets assigned buses, steadies students coming down the steps, receives handoff and any medical/behavior report from the driver, retrieves backpacks, feeding bags, or communication devices, and walks students into the building to class.

Student who uses a wheelchair or adaptive stroller: TA rolls the chair onto the bus wheelchair lift, rides/operates the lift with the driver, maneuvers the chair into the securement position inside the bus, attaches four-point tie-downs and the occupant lap/shoulder belt, checks brakes, oxygen, and positioning supports, and reverses the process at unloading.

Behavioral escalation during loading: a student refuses to board, drops to the ground, elopes toward traffic, or becomes aggressive; the TA de-escalates with prompts and preferred items, uses trained physical escort/protective holds if the student's safety requires it, and gets the student safely seated and restrained (safety vest or harness) before the bus departs.

TA assigned as bus monitor on a special-education route serving residential home stops: at each stop the TA helps a student down the steps at a curb or driveway, crosses with them, hands the student to a parent or caregiver, and manages students still on board. Layouts differ at every stop, public street traffic, snow/rain/darkness, no institutional control of the site.

sources.title: Q'Straint Introduces Revolutionary New Fully Automatic Wheelchair Securement System - School Transportation News
sources.claim: Q'Straint Quantum is an automated rear-facing wheelchair securement station installed in buses; it clamps a mobility device after the rider positions the chair and presses a button, but it does not move, escort, or restrain the occupant, and presupposes a passenger who can drive and align their own chair.
sources.transferJustification: Closest automation to the securement sub-step of bus loading. It does not transfer: it handles only a self-positioning adult rider's device, performs no escorting, no lift operation, no occupant restraint of a child who cannot self-position, and no supervision.

sources.developer: WHILL, Inc. / Aicher Airport Services, Unifi Aviation
sources.title: WHILL Launches Autonomous Services at Munich Airport
sources.claim: WHILL autonomous wheelchairs carry passengers along mapped routes inside airport terminals; airline/ground-handling staff still guide passengers to the pickup point, assist with boarding the device, and stow their bags.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: escorting/transporting a mobility-limited person inside a controlled facility. It does not transfer to bus loading of students with disabilities: humans still perform the boarding assistance, the riders are cooperative self-managing adults, and the device does no lift operation, restraint fastening, or supervision of children who may elope.

sources.title: Robotic patient transfer device launches at Ottawa hospital | CBC News
sources.claim: Able Innovations' ALTA robotic platform transfers patients between bed surfaces at the press of a ... in hospitals; it is an operator-initiated transfer device for a supine patient, not an autonomous system that escorts, supervises, or restrains ambulatory people.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine-mediated physical handling of a person. It does not transfer: it is caregiver-operated, works only on a supine patient on a fixed bed-to-bed path in a hospital room, and cannot walk a child to a curb, buckle a harness, or manage behavior.

sources.transferJustification: These are the robots actually present in special-education settings; they establish the ceiling of deployed capability there, which is seated social interaction rather than any physical handling of students during bus loading.

tasks.label: Maintain computers in classrooms and laboratories, and assist students with hardware and software use.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: During a lesson, the TA sits beside a student with a learning or physical disability and works them through educational software on a Chromebook or iPad: opens the app, logs in, guides the mouse/touchscreen hand-over-hand, re-prompts when the student stalls, adjusts volume, font size or accessibility settings.

Start and end of class device logistics: pulling 8-12 Chromebooks/tablets from a charging cart, powering them on and logging in, carrying them to students at their desks in an occupied classroom, then collecting them and returning each to its slot with the charger plugged in.

Mid-lesson hardware trouble on one student's station: no sound in the headphones, unresponsive mouse or keyboard (dead battery, loose dongle), frozen tablet, or a disconnected HDMI/USB-C lead on the interactive display. The TA diagnoses, reseats or swaps the part, restarts if needed, and gets the student back on task within a minute or two.

Setting up and maintaining assistive technology for a student with physical or communication disabilities: mounting an AAC speech device or access switch on a wheelchair tray, plugging in the switch interface and charger, calibrating eye-gaze or touch, loading the right vocabulary page set, and positioning the student's hand or head to use it.

Out-of-class cable and power upkeep in the classroom/computer lab with no students present: walking the row of stations reconnecting or reseating monitor, keyboard, mouse and headphone leads, dressing cables, and plugging every device and charger back in.

Out-of-class general upkeep of the lab with no students present: waking or restarting machines, letting pending updates and logins complete, swapping a dead mouse or batteries, checking each station's headphones, wiping screens and keyboards, and flagging broken units for the district IT technician.

tasks.label: Requisition and stock teaching materials and supplies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Delivered cartons of consumable classroom supplies (paper, crayons, markers, glue sticks, tissues, wipes) arrive in a special-education classroom; the aide opens the boxes, sorts contents, and shelves them in cabinets, closets and labeled bins, often around furniture, student work stations and students who are present.

Routine replenishment of instructional materials: refilling student work bins and task boxes with worksheets, laminated task cards, PECS/visual supports, manipulatives and adapted materials, and setting out stocked materials at learning stations for the next lesson or next day.

Inventory and requisition: walking the classroom cabinets and storage closet to see what is running low, noting quantities, then completing a paper purchase-requisition form or an online district ordering cart and submitting it to the teacher or school office.

Fetching supplies from the school's central supply room, workroom or bookroom: pulling a modest number of requested items (reams of paper, marker packs, laminating pouches, file folders) from labeled shelves/bins, loading a cart, and transporting them through corridors (sometimes an elevator) back to the classroom.

Stocking specialized and personal-care supplies used in a self-contained special-education room: gloves, wipes, pull-ups/diapers, feeding and hygiene items, sensory and adaptive equipment, placed into designated cabinets, changing-area shelves and individual student cubbies.

instances.label: School workroom/copy room: the TA is handed a stack of freshly printed letter-size sheets of picture-communication icons, sight-word cards, or visual-schedule symbols; runs them through the pouch laminator in batches, then cuts the laminated sheets apart into individual cards on the paper cutter (sometimes rounding corners) and bands them into sets.
