sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous live performance to a paying audience. Shows the ceiling of autonomous robot performance today — canned material with timing adaptation, a research demo, not sustained character portrayal.

tasks.label: Study and rehearse roles from scripts to interpret, learn and memorize lines, stunts, and cues as directed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Film/TV actor studies the script privately (home, trailer, hotel): analyzes the role, breaks down beats, memorizes next day's sides, runs lines aloud alone or with a reader/coach, marks cues, until off-book and ready to shoot.

Film/TV rehearsal on a soundstage, location set, or rehearsal hall: walking blocking to camera marks, adjusting performance to the director's notes, learning cues to lighting/camera/other actors, running the scene repeatedly until the director accepts it.

Theatre rehearsal process: weeks in a rehearsal room and then on stage, learning blocking and lines, interpreting the role under a director's notes, working scenes with a scene partner, then cue-to-cue/tech and dress rehearsals with light, sound and set cues.

Stunt, fight or dance rehearsal with a stunt coordinator/choreographer in a padded stunt gym, stage or set: learning a choreographed fight, fall, wire or harness sequence, repeating it at increasing speed, adjusting for safety and camera angle until signed off.

Voice-over/radio/commercial or animation work: studying copy or script, rehearsing line readings in a recording booth, taking the director's direction on tone and timing, hitting timing cues for the take.

Live-character, theme-park, industrial or educational performer: learning a short scripted routine, interaction beats and cues, rehearsing it in a training room or on the show site until the show director approves it.

sources.developer: University of Nottingham / Aberystwyth University (Panagiotidis et al.)
sources.title: [2508.03514] Theatre in the Loop: A Rehearsal-Based, Collaborative Workflow for Expressive Robotic Behaviours
sources.claim: State-of-the-art robot rehearsal work builds performance behaviour by having a human puppeteer improvise gestures under a director's guidance, which are then recorded as templates for later playback; the robot does not learn a role itself.
sources.transferJustification: This is the closest analogue to the rated task (a robot acquiring a performance in rehearsal under a director); it shows the acquisition is done by a human puppeteer, so it cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.system: Geminoid F / Wakamaru in Oriza Hirata's robot theatre ("Sayonara")
sources.developer: Osaka University (Ishiguro Lab) / ATR with Seinendan theatre company
sources.title: Robot Drama Research: From Identification to Synchronization
sources.claim: Androids that have played characters in staged plays did so through pre-programming or motion-capture teleoperation from a human actress, not by studying a script and learning a role.
sources.transferJustification: Directly about robots taking roles in stage plays; establishes that the interpretive/rehearsal work is supplied by humans, so the robot does not complete the rated task.

sources.title: Look, up in the sky! It's Disney's new autonomous acrobatic robot
sources.claim: Disney's Stuntronics is an autonomous aerial animatronic built to stand in for a human actor's stunt, self-correcting in mid-air using onboard sensing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing (not rehearsing/learning) a stunt. The trajectory is engineered offline by Imagineers; the robot does not learn a new stunt from a coordinator's direction, so transfer to the rated task is only partial.

sources.system: Spider-Man Stuntronic, "The Amazing Spider-Man!" show, Avengers Campus
sources.title: Additional Spider-Man Stuntronic Performances Come to Avengers Campus in Time for Holidays at the Disneyland Resort
sources.claim: A Stuntronics-derived Spider-Man robot performs a scripted aerial stunt show many times a day in a purpose-built launch-and-catch rig above a theme-park building.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: executing one fixed engineered stunt in a show. It does not study a script, take direction, or learn/adjust a routine, so it does not carry over to rehearsing stunts and cues as directed.

sources.system: Unitree H1 humanoids at the CCTV Spring Festival Gala
sources.title: Dancing kings: Unitree humanoid robots, backed by Alibaba tech, delight Spring Gala show
sources.claim: Humanoid robots can execute human-authored choreography live on a broadcast stage alongside human dancers using whole-body motion control; the choreography is engineered and retargeted by human teams beforehand.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing choreographed movement on a stage. The movement is authored and tuned by engineers rather than learned by the robot from a director's notes, so it does not substantiate the rated rehearsal/learning task.

sources.title: Ameca | Engineered Arts
sources.claim: Commercially deployed expressive humanoids used for entertainment run human-authored animations created with the vendor's animation tooling and operator-selected modes.
sources.transferJustification: Closest commercial 'performing humanoid'; its performance content is authored by humans in an animation tool, so it does not perform the study/rehearse/learn-a-role task.

tasks.label: Collaborate with other actors as part of an ensemble.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Rehearsal-room ensemble work for a stage production: table work, blocking, and repeated scene work in a rented rehearsal hall or on the theatre's stage, trying choices with scene partners, giving and taking cues, adjusting timing and physicality in response to partners and the director's notes.

Live stage performance before a paying audience in a theatre: playing scenes in real time with fellow cast members, sustaining a character, handling props and physical contact (embraces, stage combat, choreographed movement), and adapting on the spot to partners' variations, dropped lines, and audience response.

Film or TV scene work on a sound stage: performing a scene with other actors over many takes and camera setups, hitting marks, matching eyelines, sustaining and matching emotional continuity across coverage, and re-calibrating with scene partners after each directorial note.

Film or TV scene work on practical location: a real street, private house, field, or moving vehicle, with weather, traffic, bystanders, and improvised staging; the actor plays the scene with fellow cast members under conditions the production only partly controls.

Voice/audio-drama ensemble session or motion-capture volume scene work: performers in a booth or a capture stage playing a scene together, trading cues, matching energy and overlap, and reworking passages on the engineer's or director's instruction.

Live-entertainment ensemble work at a theme park, improv club, or immersive/interactive show: short repeated sets performed with other cast members before guests, requiring in-character improvisation with partners and unpredictable audience members.

sources.title: RoboThespian stars in UK play Spillikin, a love story - Robohub
sources.claim: In the professional touring production Spillikin, an Engineered Arts RoboThespian performed a role opposite human actors, but every line and movement was pre-programmed and cue-triggered by an operator, so the machine could not respond to or adjust with its scene partners.
sources.transferJustification: This is the closest available instantiation of the task itself (a robot performing in an ensemble with human actors on a theatre stage); it is cited to show that the state of the art is scripted playback with operator-triggered cues rather than ensemble collaboration.

sources.title: VIDEO: Disney Research Trains BDX Droids in Autonomous Human Interaction - WDW News Today
sources.claim: Disney Research demonstrated BDX droids learning short interactive behaviours from human-operated demonstrations and replaying them autonomously with guests; the behaviours are brief personality/mood displays, not scene work with fellow performers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: live character interaction with guests and cast members in a themed entertainment show. Cited because it is the most advanced deployed 'performing' robot; transfer to ensemble acting fails because the learned behaviours are short mood displays, not sustained roles rehearsed and adjusted with scene partners.

sources.system: BDX droids in Disney parks shows
sources.title: BDX droid | Wookieepedia
sources.claim: BDX droids are deployed in shows at Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge and on a world tour, but show sequences are driven by Imagineers remotely controlling the droids, with autonomous replay of the recorded input as the next development step.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing a live show alongside human cast members in a theme park. Cited to establish that deployed park performances remain operator-driven and involve non-human droid characters, so they do not substantiate autonomous ensemble acting.

sources.system: AI-powered humanoid robot in 'A Robotic Love Story' at Atatürk Cultural Center
sources.title: AI-powered humanoid robot takes the stage at AKM - Hürriyet Daily News
sources.claim: A 2026 Turkish production placed an AI-powered humanoid robot in an actor's role alongside human cast members at a major theatre, but no autonomy for live scene response with partners is established in the reporting.
sources.transferJustification: This is the most recent instantiation of a robot in a cast; cited to show that even the newest stage examples give no evidence of autonomous, responsive collaboration and cast the machine as a robot character.

sources.title: Researchers train 'world's most advanced humanoid robot' Ameca on GPT-4, finds her less responsive - Interesting Engineering
sources.claim: The most responsive humanoid performers available are stationary conversational busts such as Ameca, which generate unscripted spoken replies via a large language model but do not play roles, rehearse, or perform staged action with other actors.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: live unscripted verbal interaction with people. Cited as the upper bound on autonomous responsiveness; it does not transfer to ensemble acting because Ameca is immobile, plays no character arc, and cannot execute blocking, physical contact, or take-to-take continuity.

tasks.label: Learn about characters in scripts and their relationships to each other to develop role interpretations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Perform humorous and serious interpretations of emotions, actions, and situations, using body movements, facial expressions, and gestures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scene work on a soundstage or controlled interior set for film/TV: the actor plays a scripted role, hits marks under lighting, sustains an emotional beat in close-up across multiple takes, adjusts the interpretation on the director's notes, and reacts moment-to-moment to a scene partner.

Live stage performance of a play or musical before a paying audience in a theatre: a full role sustained over two hours, projected body language and facial expression readable from the back row, comic timing calibrated to audience response, recovery from missed cues or props.

Location shooting in practical, non-studio settings (city streets, private homes, fields, moving vehicles) with weather, uneven ground, crowds and noise; the actor performs the same emotional interpretation while walking, handling props and matching continuity across takes.

Commercial, corporate, industrial or instructional video work on a rented set or client site: playing a light comic or earnest 'real person' character to camera, delivering product/safety/training content with expression and gesture, taking rapid direction from an agency client.

Live interactive character work: theme-park and immersive-experience character performers, murder-mystery and dinner theatre, brand activations, improv, and touring educational/historical shows in schools and museums — unscripted, in-character reaction to guests including children, sustained over long shifts.

Performance-capture work in a mocap volume: the actor performs the emotional interpretation in a marker suit and head-mounted facial camera on a sparse stage, with the body and face performance itself being the deliverable data for an animated character.

sources.system: Disney Research robotic character (BDX-style droid) with operator-imitation policy
sources.title: [2504.02724] Autonomous Human-Robot Interaction via Operator Imitation
sources.claim: Disney Research trained a diffusion policy from teleoperator data so a robotic character can autonomously perform expressive, mood-varied interactions (happy, sad, angry, shy) with a nearby person; demonstrated in a motion-capture lab, not deployed as a park performer.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: in-character emotional expression toward a live audience via body movement. It is the closest published autonomous analogue to an actor conveying emotion through movement, but it covers only four coarse moods in short lab interactions, not a sustained interpretive role.

sources.system: BDX droids at Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge
sources.developer: Walt Disney Imagineering R&D / Disney Live Entertainment
sources.title: BDX Droids Begin Limited Run at Walt Disney World's Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge
sources.claim: The BDX droids actually deployed as characters at Disney parks are character-performed by backstage puppeteers; only balance, gait and obstacle response are machine-controlled.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: theme-park character performance. It shows that the only in-service robotic 'character actors' still depend on continuous human puppeteering for the performance itself, which the rating rules exclude.

sources.title: Ameca | Engineered Arts
sources.claim: Ameca is a commercially sold expressive humanoid used as an interactive attraction in museums and science centres; its autonomous repertoire is configurable idle behaviours and microexpressions layered onto conversation, not the performance of a dramatic role.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: expressive face-and-gesture human interaction. It is the most capable commercially deployed expressive humanoid face, yet its output is conversational behaviour selected from presets rather than an interpreted comic or dramatic role.

sources.system: Stuntronics / Aerial Stunt Robot (Spider-Man, Avengers Campus)
sources.title: Stuntronics Spider-Man in Avengers Campus!
sources.claim: Disney's Spider-Man 'Stuntronic' aerial stunt robot performs in-character acrobatic action over a theme-park plaza, using onboard sensors to correct its pose in flight; it has no face, dialogue or emotional performance and is launched and caught by a purpose-built rig.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: in-character physical action performance (stunt work). Transfer is partial only: it substitutes for a stunt double's single aerial beat in a fixed rig, and cannot produce facial expression, comic timing or an emotional interpretation.

sources.title: Comedy club performances provide insights on how robots, humans connect via humor | Oregon State University
sources.claim: An autonomous stand-up comedy robot performed routines in Los Angeles and Oregon comedy clubs, using audience-laughter sensing for adaptive timing plus arm gestures, in a research study rather than as a booked professional performer.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: humorous live performance before an audience. It is autonomous and audience-adaptive, but is a small tabletop robot delivering written jokes with token gestures, far short of an actor's embodied comic interpretation.

tasks.label: Read from scripts or books to narrate action or to inform or entertain audiences, utilizing few or no stage props.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Audiobook narration: actor sits in a recording studio or treated home booth reading a novel or nonfiction manuscript aloud for multi-hour sessions, voicing characters, pacing, and picking up corrections at the direction of a producer/engineer. No props; output is the recorded voice performance.

Voice-over narration in a booth for documentaries, corporate/e-learning modules, commercials, and explainer videos: reading supplied copy to timing and picture, adjusting tone and emphasis per director notes over several takes.

Live staged reading, readers' theater, cold reading at a new-play workshop or audition: actor stands or sits with script in hand before a live audience or creative team and reads dialogue and stage directions with minimal or no props.

Reading aloud to a live in-person group in a school, library, bookstore, or museum program — storytime, author-style book reading, or narrated educational presentation — holding a book and reading to children or a general audience.

Scripted narration for broadcast/streamed formats: radio drama, fiction podcast, on-camera or off-camera narration read from a teleprompter or script for a documentary or awards/event broadcast, delivered in a studio or on set.

tasks.label: Work with other crew members responsible for lighting, costumes, make-up, and props.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Film/TV soundstage shoot day: the actor reports to wardrobe for fitting and quick changes, sits for hair/makeup with continuity checks and touch-ups between takes, takes and hits marks laid by the gaffer/DP so lighting and focus hold, and rehearses prop business (weapons, food, phones, period objects) with the props master.

Professional stage/theatre production: fittings and alterations sessions with the costume shop, dresser-assisted quick changes in the wings, 'finding the light' and holding positions during a tech/cue-to-cue rehearsal with the LD, and setting/returning props with the run crew on the prop table per stage management's tracking.

Location shoot (city street, practical house, exterior): makeup and hair touch-ups fighting weather, wind and sweat; wardrobe adjustments and continuity between setups; hitting marks under mixed natural/portable lighting; handling props on uneven ground amid uncontrolled surroundings.

Commercial, corporate/industrial video, or small green-screen studio shoot: rapid wardrobe and makeup turnaround with a one- or two-person crew, tracking-marker and lighting constraints explained on the fly, and precise product/prop handling to the client's and prop stylist's direction.

Live broadcast studio, theme-park/live-event show, or motion-capture stage: pre-show makeup and mic/rig fitting, working to fixed-set lighting and camera positions, timed prop handoffs with stagehands, and mocap-suit/marker fitting and prop stand-in coordination with the capture crew.

sources.title: Robot Is the Star in New Play
sources.claim: RoboThespian, the humanoid robot cast in the touring play 'Spillikin', performs on stage alongside human actors but delivers fixed lines and movements played back from triggered cues rather than acting autonomously; it is a bolted-in-place torso robot that does not walk, hit marks, or handle costumes/props with crew.
sources.transferJustification: Closest existing analogue to an actor working within a production's lighting/props/costume workflow; cited to show the state of the art is cue-triggered playback, which cannot substitute for an actor's interactive collaboration with crew.

sources.developer: Hiroshi Ishiguro Laboratory / Osaka University, with Oriza Hirata
sources.title: Android Actress Takes To The Stage In Japan
sources.claim: The android Geminoid F has been cast as a stage and screen performer opposite human actors in Oriza Hirata's 'Sayonara', but the figure is an immobile seated android whose speech and gestures are operator-driven/pre-programmed, with no capability for costume fittings, makeup sessions, hitting lighting marks, or prop handling.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing a role in a theatre/film production. Cited because it is the nearest robotic 'actor' deployment; its operator-driven, immobile nature shows performance-support collaboration with crew departments is not achieved.

sources.title: BREAKING: BDX Droids Now Roaming Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge at Walt Disney World
sources.claim: Disney's BDX droids are deployed as free-roaming character performers in a controlled theme-park environment (Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge), but the park units are remote-controlled by operators, with autonomous human interaction still in research.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: live character performance in a production/show setting. Cited to establish that even the most advanced deployed robotic 'performers' rely on human operators, so they cannot supply the actor's autonomous cooperation with lighting, wardrobe and prop crews.

sources.title: NVIDIA GTC 2025: Jensen Huang Introduces AI Robot Blue. The evolution of Disney's BDX Box Droids?
sources.claim: A separate account of Disney's droid program confirms the park-deployed BDX units are remote-controlled, in contrast with research prototypes using learned control.
sources.transferJustification: Corroborates the autonomy status of the closest deployed robotic performer; supports the negative judgment that no autonomous system fills an actor's collaborative role with production crew.

sources.title: Ameca | Engineered Arts
sources.claim: Ameca is a commercially sold humanoid character robot with autonomous conversational behaviours and expressive micro-movements, but it is a stationary upper-body platform used for engagement and exhibition; it cannot be costume-fitted, made up for camera continuity, walk to lighting marks, or execute prop business on cue.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: expressive character performance and audience interaction. Cited to show autonomous entertainment humanoids exist but lack the mobility and bodily cooperation the costume/makeup/lighting/prop workflow requires.

sources.title: Figure AI's Helix-02 Robots Complete Full 8-Hour Autonomous Shifts as Humanoid Race Intensifies
sources.claim: The frontier of autonomous humanoid manipulation as of 2026 is whole-body control for industrial material handling — Figure's Helix-02 robots running multi-hour autonomous shifts in logistics/factory settings — not performer-side collaboration with wardrobe, makeup, lighting and prop departments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous whole-body manipulation in a work facility. Cited to bound the state of the art: demonstrated autonomy covers structured logistics work, with no demonstration of an embodied performer being fitted, made up, marked and prop-rehearsed with a production crew.

tasks.label: Promote productions using means such as interviews about plays or movies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Prepare and perform action stunts for motion picture, television, or stage productions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fight choreography for camera on a soundstage or controlled set: the actor or fight double rehearses and then performs punches, kicks, weapon exchanges, throws and knockdowns with a human scene partner, in costume and in character, hitting marks for close and medium coverage over many takes.

Falls, wire work and aerial acrobatics on a rigged set: high fall to an airbag, ratchet pull, descender drop, harness flight or somersaulting leap, performed in costume with the face often masked or shot at distance, on rigging set up by the stunt department.

Live theatrical stage production: staged sword fight or brawl, tumbling falls, and harness flying integrated into a scene with dialogue and fellow actors, performed in front of an audience multiple times a week with no retakes.

Theme-park or arena stunt show: a fixed, repeated high aerial gag (a leap or flight over the crowd from a building/tower into a concealed landing) run several times daily as part of a scripted costumed-character show.

Vehicle stunt gag on a closed course or closed road: precision driving, slides and drifts, near misses and chase passes coordinated with a camera car and other vehicles, driven by a stunt driver doubling for the actor.

Hazard and practical-location action: fire burns, water and underwater work, being struck or dragged by a vehicle, horse work, and costumed foot chases, climbs and rooftop/parkour running on as-found practical locations outdoors.

instances.label: Children's birthday party or private family event in a home, backyard, or rented party room: the clown arrives in full costume and makeup and delivers 45-60 minutes of interactive entertainment for 8-25 excited children - slapstick bits, magic tricks, balloon animals made to request, games, name-by-name teasing - improvising continuously around a chaotic group and the parents' expectations.

Roving/walk-around clowning at a parade, street fair, festival, or storefront promotion: costumed and made up, the performer moves through outdoor crowds on uneven pavement or grass, does short gags, mock-chases and prop bits with strangers of all ages, hands out balloons, and reacts to weather, noise and hecklers.

Rehearsed clown act in a circus ring, theatre, or variety show: a 5-10 minute costumed entree with prop gags (pratfalls, pie/water bit, oversized props), timed to music and to other performers, repeated over several shows a day on a stage or ring prepared by the venue, with only brief scripted audience participation.

Hospital, hospice, or nursing-home clown visit: in a soft costume and light makeup, the performer moves room to room in a pediatric or geriatric ward, improvises gentle comedy with individual patients, reads the mood of sick children and staff, and works around beds, IV poles and infection-control rules.

Costumed comic character work at a theme park, family restaurant, mall, school assembly, or corporate event: roving or short-set gags, photos with guests, balloon twisting and crowd-pleasing physical comedy inside a venue whose operator controls the premises and schedules the performances.

Pre- and post-show preparation: applying full clown makeup (whiteface/auguste greasepaint, mouth and eye lines) to one's own face at a dressing-room mirror, fitting wig, nose, oversized shoes and costume, checking props, then removing makeup afterward.

tasks.label: Construct puppets and ventriloquist dummies, and sew accessory clothing, using hand tools and machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Building the soft body/skin of a one-off hand or rod puppet in the performer's home workshop or small studio: cutting the performer's own pattern from fleece/antron, carving and gluing a foam core, sewing curved 3D seams by machine and hand, fitting a mouth plate, turning and covering, gluing fur and features.

Making the head/face: sculpting or carving foam, basswood or clay (or casting from a mold), hollowing and sanding, installing eyes and a hinged mouth, then sealing, painting and finishing to a character design; done on a bench in a home or small studio shop.

Ventriloquist dummy mechanical build: fabricating and fitting the headstick, jaw linkage, eye/eyebrow and mouth mechanisms, control lever and strings, and joining head, torso and limbs with hand tools and small power tools; one-off, fitted by trial and adjustment.

Sewing simple accessory clothing for a puppet or dummy - shirt, trousers, tunic, cape - from a flat paper pattern in woven or knit fabric on a domestic sewing machine, with straight and curved seams and hems.

Elaborate costume and accessory work: trims, linings, collars, closures (snaps, hook-and-loop, buttons), hats, shoes and hand-finished detail, fitted and adjusted on the puppet's irregular, non-standard body.

Repair and refit of existing puppets between rehearsals and performances, backstage or in the production's shop: re-stitching split seams, re-gluing fur and foam, replacing worn rods, hinges and hardware, patching and re-dyeing to match.

sources.title: Sewbotsu00ae - Softwear Automation

tasks.label: Perform original and stock tricks of illusion to entertain and mystify audiences, occasionally including audience members as participants.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Close-up/strolling magic at a booked private or corporate event (wedding reception, holiday party, restaurant or bar). The performer works table to table within arm's reach of spectators, doing card, coin, rubber-band and ring routines, borrowing spectators' rings, phones and bills, improvising patter, reading reactions, and repeating a rotating set for dozens of small groups amid noise, drink glasses and variable lighting.

Booked stage or parlor act (theater, casino showroom, cruise-ship lounge, corporate banquet stage): a 20-60 minute routine with large props and illusion boxes, an assistant, music and light cues, patter and comedy, and volunteers invited up from the audience whose unpredictable behavior must be managed while the method is concealed.

Family/children's show at a birthday party in a private home or backyard, or in a school gym, library room or church hall: portable prop case, a 30-45 minute routine, children handled as on-stage participants, heavy improvisation, crowd control and noise, a different room layout at every booking.

Trade-show booth, brand activation or fixed attraction gig: the same tight 5-10 minute routine repeated dozens of times per day from a fixed table/stand with the performer's own pre-set props (no borrowed objects required), drawing and amusing passersby, usually with one volunteer picking a card or holding an object.

Street/festival busking on a public pitch or plaza: build a crowd from passersby, work outdoors in wind, sun and noise, recruit volunteers from strangers, handle hecklers and interruptions, and close with a hat line.

Televised, filmed or streamed magic segment shot in a TV studio or on location: camera-angle-dependent effects, multiple takes, blocking to marks, working an effect on a host, celebrity or small studio audience under lights and direction.

sources.claim: A purpose-built four-fingered card-dealing robot performs a complete card trick with audience participation on a fixed bench setup: the spectator starts and stops the deal, and the robot switches between first- and second-card dealing faster than a human magician so the final card is always the Ace.

tasks.label: Test equipment to ensure proper operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-show/pre-record technical check of a TV studio and control room before a newscast or taping: power up and confirm cameras (shading/registration, focus, tally, robotic presets), mics and console channels, IFB/intercom, teleprompter, switcher/graphics/replay, record devices and return feeds; sign off that the studio is air-ready under a hard clock. Institution-controlled studio, fixed layout, people present.

Radio station on-air studio and air-chain check: speak into and level each studio mic, exercise console faders and monitor/headphone feeds, verify playout automation, phone hybrid/codec, audio processing, off-air monitoring and a weekly EAS test; confirm audio actually reaches the transmitter path. Institution-controlled station facility.

Field/remote production check before an ENG or OB shoot: at a stadium, arena, parking lot, or news scene, confirm camera and lens function, run and test cable, scan RF and verify wireless mics/comms, test the bonded-cellular or satellite uplink and confirm the station's return feed, working in weather and around a layout taken as found.

Bench test of an individual item in the engineering shop or rack room: a camera head, lens, wireless pack, microphone, monitor, power supply, converter card, or cable is brought in; connect it to test signal generator/waveform monitor/audio analyzer, power it up, exercise its inputs and outputs, measure against spec and declare pass/fail or route for repair.

Routine plant round of the rack room, master control machine room, or transmitter site: walk a fixed route, confirm units are powered and within normal parameters, read transmitter/UPS meters and status displays, check cooling and rack temperatures, listen for fan or bearing anomalies, log readings and flag anything abnormal.

Hands-on facility infrastructure test: exercise the standby generator and transfer switch, load-test the UPS, verify satellite dish/antenna pointing and reflected power, verify and re-patch cable plant or fiber links, physically reset or reseat equipment found faulty during the check.

sources.system: Averna end-of-line (EOL) robotic functional test cells
sources.title: End-of-Line (EOL) Testing Solutions | Averna
sources.claim: Averna builds end-of-line functional test systems in which industrial robots (Mecademic, FANUC, Stäubli, Epson) position and connect units under test in purpose-built fixtures, run functional/electrical verification and report results; commercially deployed test cells.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: end-of-line functional testing of electronic products. It is the same act as a broadcast engineer's bench test — power the unit, exercise its interfaces, measure against spec, declare pass/fail — on comparable electronic assemblies, and it is done with the unit fixtured and presented to the machine, which is exactly the E1 counterfactual.

sources.system: Takaya APT-1600FD / APT-1400F flying probe test systems
sources.title: TAKAYA APT-1600FD Dual-side Flying Probe Test - Accelonix
sources.claim: Takaya APT-series flying probe testers autonomously drive multiple moving probes over an assembled electronic board to make electrical measurements and detect faults, and run in fully automated in-line or magazine-to-magazine operation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: electrical verification of assembled electronics. Broadcast bench testing of a card, power supply or converter is the same class of work — contact the device, apply stimulus, measure R/L/C, voltages and signal behaviour, and judge pass/fail — with the workpiece clamped and presented by a conveyor, i.e. an E1 presentation.

sources.system: Robotic functional-test (FCT) handling cells in electronics manufacturing
sources.title: Electronics Manufacturing Robotics: SMT, Assembly & Testing Automation | Seraphim
sources.claim: Industry description of robotic functional-test automation: robotic handlers load electronic assemblies into test fixtures, make the electrical connections, run the test sequence and sort pass/fail units.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: functional test of electronic assemblies. tasks.label: Maintain equipment used in a particular sport.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Post-practice/post-game care of personal gear in a team locker room or equipment room: wiping down helmet, pads and shoes, airing out and hanging soaked gear to dry, washing/drying practice kit, restocking and stowing the bag in a locker. Many small varied items, no fixturing, done in the few minutes after a session.

Consumable and wear-part upkeep on hand implements, mostly done seated in a locker room, hotel room, or at home: taping a hockey stick blade and knob, re-gripping a golf club/bat/racquet handle, oiling and re-lacing a baseball glove, replacing spikes/cleats and laces, waxing a board, tightening screws on bindings or blades.

Mechanical upkeep of wheeled/mechanical sport equipment by cyclists, triathletes, BMX/skate and motocross competitors: degreasing and lubing the drivetrain, checking tire pressure or changing a tube, adjusting brakes and derailleurs, torquing bolts, cleaning bearings — done in a home garage, team truck, or pit area with hand tools on the athlete's own machine.

Blade and base servicing done on shop machines in a rink equipment room, pro shop or wax room: sharpening/profiling skate blades to a chosen hollow, and grinding, edge-tuning and hot-waxing skis or snowboards, then checking the edges/base before use.

Stringing work: restringing or replacing strings and overgrips on a tennis/badminton/squash racquet, or restringing a lacrosse head pocket, at a club stringing bench or at home, weaving and tensioning string to the athlete's chosen tension and pattern.

Pre-event inspection and preparation of the competition kit at the venue: checking helmets, pads, straps, laces and fasteners for damage, replacing worn parts, adjusting equipment to the rules/spec for the event, and packing the bag so everything needed is present and serviceable.

sources.title: Pro Skate Sharpening – Simmons Hockey

tasks.label: Attend scheduled practice or training sessions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Team-sport athlete (football, basketball, soccer, hockey, baseball) attends a scheduled on-field/on-court practice at the club's training facility: warm-up, position drills run to a coach's instructions, situational reps and full-speed scrimmage against teammates, with contact, tactical adjustments and coach feedback.

Athlete attends a scheduled strength-and-conditioning session in the team weight room or performance center: barbell and machine lifts to prescribed loads, plyometrics, sprint/agility work and mobility, supervised by a strength coach who monitors form and adjusts loads.

Individual-sport or specialist athlete attends scheduled technical skill practice in a controlled venue: batting cage, bullpen, tennis court, driving range, pool lane, rink, mat or ring, doing repetition work against a coach, ball machine or sparring partner at competitive intensity.

Athlete attends a scheduled training session held on location outdoors: road cycling or trail running miles on public roads, open-water swim, ski or motocross course session, in weather taken as found and among traffic or other users.

Athlete attends a scheduled non-field training session mandated as part of practice: film review, playbook walkthrough or classroom installation session at the facility, occasionally including slow-speed physical walkthrough of assignments.

sources.developer: Shenzhen Honor Smart Technology Development Co., Ltd.
sources.title: Humanoid robot surpasses human half-marathon world record in Beijing-Xinhua
sources.claim: A humanoid robot completed a 21.1 km half-marathon course under autonomous navigation in 50:26 at the 2026 Beijing E-Town event, showing that bipedal endurance locomotion on a closed road course is now machine-feasible.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: competitive road running on a closed, marshalled course. It shows locomotion capability but not attendance at an athlete's practice: a robot's run produces no conditioning, skill acquisition or coach-directed development for the human athlete whose training session it is, and the course is separated from human runners.

sources.system: DeepMind table tennis robot (ABB arm with learned hierarchical policies)
sources.title: Google DeepMind develops a 'solidly amateur' table tennis robot | TechCrunch
sources.claim: The most advanced learned robot racket-sport agent plays at solidly amateur level: it beat all beginners, split matches with intermediates and lost every match to advanced players, well below the standard of a competitive athlete's practice reps.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: competitive racket-sport rallying, the closest analogue to an athlete's skill-practice reps. Performance caps at amateur level in a fixed, instrumented lab setting, so it does not carry over to professional-level technical practice.

sources.system: World Humanoid Robot Games 5v5 humanoid soccer (Unitree-class humanoids)
sources.title: World's first humanoid robot games playing 5v5 soccer qualifiers in Beijing
sources.claim: Fully autonomous humanoid robot soccer reached only 5v5 matches on a purpose-built robot pitch in 2025, with prior events limited to 3v3 — far below the speed, contact and tactical complexity of a professional team practice.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: playing team soccer, the direct analogue of scrimmage work in a team practice. Robots play a slow, simplified game on a marked robot field, so capability does not transfer to full-speed professional practice.

sources.system: Mobile Virtual Player (MVP) mobile tackling dummy
sources.title: Steelers experimenting with robot tackling dummies
sources.claim: Robots that do appear at professional practices function as training equipment rather than as athletes: the Mobile Virtual Player used by NFL clubs is a remote-controlled padded tackling dummy that players hit, not a participant that trains in a player's place.
sources.transferJustification: Same setting (an NFL practice field) but a different role: the machine is a teleoperated drill aid absorbing contact, which does not substitute for an athlete attending and executing the practice.

instances.label: In-season individength--supervised strength and conditioning session in the team's or a commercial performance gym: barbell lifts, machines, plyometrics, mobility work, following a prescribed program and logging loads.
Sport-specific conditioning/practice session at the team facility  ield: — sprint work, skating drills, swim sets, on-court conditioning, executed at prescribed intensity and volume.
Following the nutrition and recovery plan day to day: preparing or selecting meals, hydration, supplement timing, sleep, and body-composition checks at home, in hotels, and on the road.

Consulting with health professionals: attending appointments with the team physician, dietitian, physiotherapist or athletic trainer for assessment, treatment, and program adjustment in a clinic or training room.
Off-season, travel, or independent conditioning in unstructured settings: road runs, hill or trail work, hotel-gym or home workouts, altitude camps, with variable equipment and weather.

sources.system: Rethink Robotics Baxter exergame system (and NAO/Pepper exercise buddies)
sources.title: Frontiers | How should robots exercise with people? Robot-mediated exergames win with music, social analogues, and gameplay clarity
sources.claim: Robots used in exercise contexts act as coaches or exergame partners for a human who does the exercising; the Baxter humanoid was programmed with exercise games a user plays with the robot.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-mediated exercise coaching. It does NOT transfer: the robot prompts a human to exercise, whereas this task's accepted output is the athlete's own conditioned physiology, which no machine can produce in the athlete's place.

sources.developer: Beijing Innovation Center of Human Robotics
sources.title: Humans Still Tops: Results of the Human Versus Robot Half Marathon in Beijing – iRunFar
sources.claim: Humanoid robots can locomote athletically (completing a half marathon course), but they do so as machines competing, not as a substitute producing a human athlete's fitness; performance remains far below human athletes.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: long-distance robot locomotion. It does NOT transfer: robot endurance running does not maintain any human athlete's fitness, and the robot's own upkeep is machine maintenance, a different task with a different output.

tasks.label: Participate in athletic events or competitive sports, according to established rules and regulations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Play a full regulation team ball-sport game (basketball, football, baseball, ice hockey, soccer) at professional or minor-league level in an arena or stadium: contested play against opposing athletes, officials enforcing the rulebook, coaches substituting, a scoreboard result the club is paid for.

Compete in a dual/individual contest against a live opponent in a controlled venue: a boxing or MMA bout in a ring/cage, a wrestling match, a tennis or racquet match - reacting to an adversary in real time under a referee and weight/scoring rules.

Compete in an individual timed or judged event at a standard institutional venue: a track meet in a stadium, a swim meet, velodrome racing, gymnastics or figure skating, or a golf tournament round - fixed regulation facilities and equipment, elite marks required to place.

Compete in an event held on terrain taken as found: road/marathon racing on closed city streets, cross-country, road cycling, alpine skiing, surfing, motocross or rodeo - variable course, weather, crowds and footing, over a course often seen for the first time on race day.

Drive in a motorsport event at a purpose-built circuit or oval (stock car, open-wheel, sprint car): qualifying then wheel-to-wheel racing among a field of other competitors, pit stops, race control and flags, damage-free finish expected.

sources.system: Booster K1 / Booster T1 humanoid soccer robots (B-Human, HTWK, Tsinghua Hephaestus teams)
sources.developer: Booster Robotics with university RoboCup teams
sources.title: Robots swept RoboCup 2026, and they want the human World Cup
sources.claim: The most advanced autonomous humanoid soccer robots played the first 11-vs-11 match on a real field at RoboCup 2026; the field's own stated goal is only to reach human world-champion level by 2050, i.e. robot play remains far below professional human soccer.
sources.transferJustification: Direct analogue: robot soccer matches are the closest existing form of participating in a team ball-sport game under established rules; cited to show the ceiling of current capability, not to support a positive judgment.

sources.system: DeepMind table tennis robot (ABB IRB 1100 arm on linear gantries)
sources.title: Google DeepMind develops a 'solidly amateur' table tennis robot | TechCrunch
sources.claim: The best published sport-playing robot arm reaches only amateur human level in table tennis: it beat beginners, split with intermediates, and lost every match to advanced players.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: competitive racquet play against a live human opponent under match rules, the same demand as the dual-contest instance; it bounds achievable quality against skilled human competitors.

sources.system: Tien Kung Ultra, Unitree H1 / G1
sources.developer: Beijing Innovation Center of Human Robotics; Unitree Robotics
sources.title: Inaugural World Humanoid Robot Games step into the spotlight - The Robot Report
sources.claim: At the first World Humanoid Robot Games, humanoids racing on an athletics track ran the 100 m in roughly 21.5-24.5 s and the 1500 m in about 6:34 - far off elite human marks - and the field mixed autonomous and remotely controlled entries.
sources.transferJustification: Direct analogue of a track meet event held in a stadium; shows the performance level and the mixed autonomy of the best current running humanoids.

sources.title: A humanoid robot beat the human half-marathon record at a Beijing race. But what did it actually prove? | Scientific American
sources.claim: At the 2026 Beijing E-Town humanoid half marathon the winning robot ran 50:26, but the course was dedicated and rehearsed with support crews, most entries were remotely piloted, and the winner hit a barricade, fell and had to be set upright by staff.
sources.transferJustification: Direct analogue of a road-race instance; the fall requiring hands-on human assistance and the premapped robot-only course show the event was not completed under the runner's competition conditions.

sources.system: A2RL EAV-25 autonomous Super Formula racecar (TUM and other teams)
sources.developer: ASPIRE / Technology Innovation Institute, Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League
sources.title: Abu Dhabi's autonomous racing league heads to Imola for first international test | The National
sources.claim: Fully autonomous racecars now run wheel-to-wheel races at Yas Marina in the A2RL series, but as of the 2025 season they were still about 1.58 s per lap slower than the human reference driver in the same car.
sources.transferJustification: Direct analogue of the motorsport instance: a full race format at a circuit driven by machine; the remaining lap-time deficit measures the gap to professional-driver quality.

sources.system: Unitree G1 kickboxing (China Media Group 'Iron Fist King' event)
sources.title: Unitree humanoid robots battle it out in kickboxing competition
sources.claim: Humanoid combat-sport matches staged to date are human-teleoperated rather than autonomous.
sources.transferJustification: Direct analogue of the combat-sport instance; being teleoperated, it cannot support a positive judgment under the autonomy rule.

sources.developer: University of Zurich Robotics and Perception Group with Intel
sources.title: High-speed AI drone beats world champions in drone racing
sources.claim: An autonomous quadrotor beat human world champions in first-person-view drone racing on a fixed indoor track, winning 15 of 25 races, but it required training on that specific track and failed when conditions differed from training.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine-mediated racing against champion human competitors. It is the only case of a machine beating champion humans in a sport, but it is a purpose-built pre-mapped drone track, not a race among a field of cars, so it does not transfer to the motorsport instance.

tasks.label: Exercise or practice under the direction of athletic trainers or professional coaches to develop skills, improve physical condition, or prepare for competitions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Team-sport practice session at the club/college training facility: the athlete runs coach-directed drills, positional reps and scrimmages on a field or court, adapting to whistled instruction, teammates and opponents, for 1.5-3 hours.

Strength-and-conditioning session in the team weight room under a strength coach: prescribed lifts, plyometrics, sled/sprint work at prescribed loads and tempos, aimed at increasing the athlete's own strength, power and durability.

Individual technical skill work in a sport-specific venue (batting cage, tennis court, pool lane, ice rink, driving range, mat room) with a skill coach correcting technique rep by rep and prescribing adjustments.
Outdoor conditioning taken as found: coach-prescribed road runs, hill repeats, trail work or long training rides on public roads and paths, in variable weather, traffic and terrain.

Athletic-trainer-directed rehab/prehab session in the training room: mobility work, corrective and rehabilitation exercises, return-to-play progressions, with the trainer grading pain, range of motion and readiness.

sources.system: Google DeepMind competitive table tennis robot (ABB IRB 1100 arm)

sources.claim: The most capable autonomous sport-playing robot reaches only amateur human level in a single, highly constrained sport (table tennis), on a fixed table with a fixed ball and no coach-directed skill program.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: playing a racket sport against humans. It is the closest robotic analogue to an athlete executing sport skills in practice; its ceiling (amateur, single-stroke domain, fixed table) shows the gap to professional coach-directed skill work.

sources.title: Beijing hosts world's first half-marathon for humanoid robots
sources.claim: Best-in-class humanoid endurance locomotion: the winning robot needed three battery swaps and a human handler to finish a half marathon in 2h40m, far below competitive human standards.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sustained outdoor running, the core of athletic conditioning work. Endurance, terrain handling and reliance on handlers fall far short of an athlete's prescribed road session.

instances.label: Youth or school team practice on a field, court, or gym floor: the coach gathers players and explains the rules of the game and the purpose of a drill, walks through positioning and play assignments, and gives verbal cues on footwork and body position while athletes execute.

One-on-one or small-group skill lesson (tennis, golf, swimming, gymnastics, pitching): the coach observes an athlete's technique, explains the mechanical principle behind the correction, and gives verbal/visual cues (sometimes with video replay) about hand, foot, and body positioning until the movement changes.

Classroom or film-room session with a high school, college, or club team: the coach presents the playbook, opponent tendencies, rules changes and officiating points of emphasis, and game strategy using video, whiteboard, or tablet, and questions athletes to check understanding.

In-competition instruction: sideline, dugout, bench, or mat-side coaching during games and meets, where the coach calls out strategic adjustments, reminds athletes of rules situations, and corrects technique between plays, points, or rotations under time pressure and crowd noise.

Strength, conditioning, and injury-prevention instruction in a weight room or training area: the coach explains lifting and movement principles, cues joint and limb positions, and corrects unsafe form for individuals and groups.

tasks.label: Coordinate travel arrangements and travel with team to away contests.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High school coach handles pre-trip logistics for a regular-season away game: submits bus/transportation requests to the athletic director and district transportation office, confirms departure and release times with the front office and teachers, arranges a meal stop or pre-orders food, collects and files permission/eligibility paperwork, prints and hands out itineraries to athletes and parents, and confirms details with the host school's AD. Occurs in the school office/gym over phone, email and paper forms.

Departure day at the home school: coach meets the team in the gym/parking lot at the set time, takes roll and accounts for every athlete, supervises loading of uniforms, equipment bags, water coolers, medical kit and video gear onto the bus/van, then rides with the team on public roads to the away site, keeping order, handling phones/behavior, distributing pre-game food, and troubleshooting late arrivals, traffic delays or a sick athlete en route.

Arrival and return at an unfamiliar host school: coach leads the team off the bus, checks in with the host AD, finds the assigned locker room and field/court, stages equipment and coolers, keeps athletes together in a building whose layout the coach has not seen, then after the contest reassembles the team, accounts for gear, reloads the bus, and on return to the home school supervises unloading and dismissal to waiting parents.

Multi-day/overnight trip (college, prep or travel-club team): coach or coaching staff books hotel room blocks and makes room assignments, books charter bus or team flights, handles airport check-in and oversized equipment bags, arranges team meals and per-diem, runs bed checks and curfew in hotel corridors, and shepherds a large group with gear through airports, restaurants and hotels in an unfamiliar city.

Youth/club coach with no institutional support: organizes a parent carpool caravan by group text, sends directions to an unfamiliar public park or community complex, drives to the site personally, meets and counts players at a field with variable parking and layout, carries balls/cones/first-aid kit from car to sideline, and supervises kids until parents collect them afterward.

sources.title: Digit Deployed at GXO in Historic Humanoid RAAS Agreement | Agility
sources.claim: The frontier of deployed autonomous humanoid mobile manipulation is repetitive tote handling inside a fixed logistics facility, not accompanying and supervising people through varied travel settings.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: warehouse tote induction and material movement. Cited to bound the frontier of deployed autonomous humanoid work: it is fixed-route material handling in a mapped, institution-controlled warehouse, and does not cover chaperoning athletes, handling paperwork, or managing an away-game trip.

sources.title: Waymo launching driverless robotaxis in 5 more cities
sources.claim: Fully driverless vehicles now carry passengers on public roads at commercial scale, which covers the pure transport leg but not the coach's coordination, roll-taking, gear handling or supervision duties.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous passenger transport on public roads. It substantiates only that machine-driven road travel is possible; the coach's task is coordinating arrangements and supervising a team in transit, which the vehicle does not perform.

Multi-day youth summer sports camp (soccer, basketball, baseball): coach books facility, handles registration/waivers/staffing and equipment, then each day sets up stations, demonstrates skills, groups and rotates 30-100 children of mixed ages, feeds balls, corrects technique, manages behavior, hydration and injuries.

Showcase/combine-style event or off-season skills clinic for recruiting: coach arranges venue, timing gear and registration, runs measurable tests (sprints, jumps, agility, throwing), directs athletes through stations, and compiles results/evaluations for scouts and college staff.

sources.title: Forget Ball Machines – This AI Tennis Robot Actually Rallies Back

sources.transferJustification: Related task (providing hitting repetitions in a private lesson) is partially automated, but the robot does not arrange the lesson, demonstrate or physically correct technique, or manage multiple athletes, so it does not carry over to conducting skill-improvement courses.

sources.title: World's first robotic personal trainer guides gym-goers through exercise programme

sources.transferJustification: Related task (coaching an individual through an exercise bout) is the nearest 'conducting' demonstration, but it is a lab prototype with unverified autonomy that neither sets up equipment nor runs multi-athlete sports activities.

instances.label: Team strength-and-conditioning session in a high school or college weight room: the coach explains and demonstrates barbell/dumbbell lifts (squat, bench, clean), how to load and clip plates, adjust machine seats and pins, and how to spot, to a group of 10-30 athletes of mixed experience; must show correct body mechanics, cue faults, and enforce safety.

Practice-field or gym session with sport-specific training equipment: coach explains and demonstrates use of blocking sleds, tackling dummies, pitching/ball machines, batting tees, hurdles, agility ladders, rebounders, jump ropes, resistance sleds; sets the equipment up, performs the movement at competition tempo, and corrects athletes' attempts.

Club gymnastics, cheer or diving gym: coach explains and demonstrates trampoline/tumble-track bouncing, mat and pit safety, apparatus (beam, bars, vault, springboard) settings, and spotting belts/harness rigs to youth athletes, performing the skill or a lead-up drill and physically spotting the first repetitions.

Youth/recreational league practice at a public park, community field or rented space: coach explains and demonstrates cones, agility rings, small hurdles, kids' balls and athlete-owned gear to children and parents; layout varies week to week, equipment is mismatched, weather and bystanders are uncontrolled.

Private or small-group lesson at a client's home gym, garage, batting cage or rented court: coach explains and demonstrates specialty gear (resistance bands, weighted balls, sleds, ball machines, launch monitors/radar, kettlebells) fitted to one athlete's level and to whatever equipment the client owns.

Team facility session on conditioning and monitoring equipment: coach explains and demonstrates treadmills, bikes, rowers, foam rollers, and how to fit and operate heart-rate straps, GPS vests, and timing gates, showing athletes how to wear, start and read the devices.

instances.label: Daily practice/game set-out and take-down: a school or club coach wheels ball carts, bags of balls, cones, agility ladders, hurdles, pinnies, nets and blocking/tackling dummies out of the equipment cage onto the gym floor or athletic field, positions them for drills, then gathers, wipes down and returns everything to storage afterward.

Court/range ball handling in racquet and golf instruction: a tennis, pickleball, padel or golf coach puts out ball hoppers or baskets and, during and after lessons and drills, gathers the loose balls scattered across the club court or driving range and returns them to the ball supply for the next session.

Season-start issuance and season-end collection of standardized kit (game jerseys, shorts, practice tops, warmups, team-issue balls and bags) to a roster of 20-60 athletes in a locker room or equipment room, with a per-athlete record of who received which numbered item, and check-in of returns at season's end.

Fitting and issuing sized or protective gear to individual athletes: sizing and adjusting football helmets and shoulder pads, hockey skates and pads, wrestling headgear, bats and shoes, checking fit and safety on the athlete's body and swapping items until each athlete is properly outfitted.

Selecting and acquiring: reviewing what is worn out or short, comparing vendor catalogs and quotes against a budget, submitting the purchase order through the athletic department, then receiving the cartons when they arrive, unpacking them, checking contents against the packing slip and stocking the equipment room shelves and bins.

Upkeep and off-site handling: periodic inventory counts and condition checks in the cage, inflating balls, cleaning and minor repairs, reorganizing shelves and discarding unsafe gear; plus loading and unloading gear onto the bus, van or trailer for away games, and for volunteer/youth coaches, storing the team's gear in a home garage or car trunk and hauling it to a public park field.

roles.title: Umpires, Referees, and Other Sports Officials
roles.description: Officiate at competitive athletic or sporting events. Detect infractions of rules and decide penalties according to established regulations. Includes all sporting officials, referees, and competition judges.
roles.sector: Arts, design, entertainment, sports, and media

tasks.label: Officiate at sporting events, games, or competitions, to maintain standards of play and to ensure that game rules are observed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Officiating a high school or youth basketball game in a school gym: two- or three-person crew running the floor with live play, sounding the whistle on fouls and violations, physically retrieving and handing/bouncing the ball to inbounders and free-throw shooters, administering the ball at each dead ball, reporting fouls to the table, and stepping between players to defuse confrontations, amid crowd noise and coach protests.

Officiating a youth/recreational or high school soccer match on an outdoor field taken as found (park or school field, variable turf, weather, wind, sun, spectators on the touchline): center referee runs with play for 80-90 minutes, judges fouls/offside with an assistant, issues cards, positions or re-spots the ball for restarts, marks wall distance, checks player equipment mid-match, and manages dissent.

Umpiring an amateur baseball or softball game: plate umpire sets up behind the catcher, calls balls and strikes on live pitches, handles the ball supply and hands new balls to the pitcher, dusts the plate, rules on swings, tags, and fair/foul; base umpire rotates on batted balls and makes safe/out calls at contact-prone bases, with foul balls and thrown bats as hazards.

Officiating a high school or youth tackle football game as part of a 4-6 person crew: spotting the ball after every play (including digging it out of a pile and setting forward progress), throwing flags, marking penalty enforcement by stepping off yardage, coordinating the chain crew, and unpiling/separating players between snaps on a marked field.

Refereeing a combat or contact individual sport (wrestling dual meet, youth boxing, judo/jiu-jitsu, amateur MMA card): the official kneels on the mat to view a pin, physically repositions or separates competitors, breaks clinches, stops the bout by physically intervening when a competitor is in danger, signals points, and raises the winner's hand.

Serving as a judge or stationed official at a scored or measured competition in a fixed venue (gymnastics or diving judge, swim meet stroke-and-turn official, volleyball first/second referee on the stand, track field-event judge): the official watches from an assigned station, scores or rules on legality, signals infractions, and handles equipment/measurement duties at the station.

sources.title: MLB to use ABS Challenge System starting in 2026
sources.claim: MLB's Automated Ball-Strike system is a camera/tracking system that only supplies strike-zone rulings on challenge; a human home-plate umpire still makes, signals and administers every call on the field. It is a sensing/computing system, not a physically embodied robot.
sources.transferJustification: Closest existing automation of in-game officiating judgment; cited to show the state of the art is a fixed camera system advising a human official, with no machine performing the on-field officiating role.

sources.title: Updated semi-automated offside technology will be introduced at World Cup as FIFA promise quicker decisions
sources.claim: FIFA's updated semi-automated offside technology at the 2026 World Cup sends audio alerts to human match officials' earpieces; the human referee and assistants still make and communicate the decisions and perform all on-field duties.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (soccer officiating) at the highest level of investment; shows automation is limited to advisory sensing, with no robot occupying the referee role on the pitch.

sources.title: NFL Implements Sony Hawk-Eye for First Downs
sources.claim: Even in the NFL, where Sony Hawk-Eye replaced the chain gang for measuring the line to gain, the physical act of spotting the ball after each play remains a human official's job.
sources.transferJustification: Directly addresses the football-officiating instance: the automated element is measurement only; the manipulation-and-judgment step of ball spotting has no machine substitute.

sources.title: Humanoid robot Atlas delivers match ball during Brazil v Norway FIFA World Cup game
sources.claim: The most advanced humanoid robot appearing at a live professional sporting event in 2026 performed a ceremonial pitchside ball hand-off to the human referee, not any officiating function; its role was a sponsor demonstration and its control mode was not disclosed.
sources.transferJustification: Frontier humanoid mobility in an actual stadium; cited to bound capability - the robot's role was a scripted ball delivery to a human referee, far short of officiating live play.

sources.title: Humanoid robot surprises scientists by mastering key basketball skills
sources.claim: Frontier humanoid athletic ball skills (dribbling, passing, shooting) have been shown only in laboratory demonstrations, not in officiating or live competition among human athletes.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (handling a basketball while moving among people) shows the physical frontier is lab-bound single-skill demos, so no system approaches an official's whole-game duties amid moving human players.

tasks.label: Inspect game sites for compliance with regulations or safety requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Indoor gym pre-game inspection before a high school or youth basketball game: official walks the court checking for wet/slick spots, dust and debris, loose floorboards, condition of rims, nets and backboards, wall/standard padding, bleacher and table placement relative to sidelines, working clock/scoreboard, and legal game balls; problems are reported to home management for correction before tip-off, with teams warming up and spectators already in the building.

Indoor apparatus/equipment compliance check for volleyball or wrestling: measure net height with a net chain/measuring device at center and sidelines, check net tension, antennae, standards and referee-stand padding; or inspect the wrestling mat for tears, gaps between mats, taped seams, cleanliness and clearance around the mat. Requires physical contact and precise measurement.

Outdoor field-sport inspection at a school/college stadium or maintained complex (soccer, football, lacrosse): walk the playing surface for holes, divots, exposed sprinkler heads, rocks and debris; check goal nets for holes, goals for proper anchoring (push/pull test), corner flags/pylons, goalpost padding, markings, benches and sideline clearance; assess weather, lighting and surface wetness for playability.

Baseball/softball diamond inspection at a maintained school or league field: bases secure and correctly spaced, pitching rubber and plate area, mound condition, foul lines, holes in outfield fence and protruding hardware, backstop, dugout condition, warning track, standing water, plus checking supplied game balls and on-field equipment.

Youth/recreational game at a public park or improvised site taken as found: no groundskeeper, layout varies, glass/trash/animal waste on the grass, uneven ground, unanchored or tip-prone portable goals, faded or missing lines, adjacent hazards (trees, curbs, parked cars); official must judge whether the site can be played on and what must be moved or modified.

sources.title: Spot at Cargill | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot performs routine autonomous inspection rounds including visual safety checks at Cargill's Amsterdam oilseed crush and refinery plant, walking pre-taught routes and flagging hazards for staff.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: recurring facility safety-compliance inspection. Like a pre-game site check it means traversing a work area, comparing what is seen against a fixed list of required conditions, and reporting deviations - but only against checkpoints registered in advance for that one site.

sources.title: Boston Dynamics Robot Dog Spot Inspects for Safety Hazards | AI Business
sources.claim: The Cargill deployment's checks are explicitly safety-compliance items: slip and trip hazards, doors left open, safety signage and fire extinguishers present and functional.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: presence/condition checks of fixed safety items, comparable to a referee verifying padding, nets and equipment are in place; the robot's checks are configured per checkpoint rather than open-ended hazard judgement.

sources.title: Quadruped robot boosts safety and maintenance at aging cement plant | Interesting Engineering
sources.claim: ANYbotics' ANYmal has run autonomous inspection rounds at a cement plant since early 2025, completing more than 33,000 inspections using onboard perception and navigation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: repeated autonomous inspection rounds over a fixed route with pre-registered inspection points - the closest deployed analogue to a repeated pre-event venue check when the checkpoints are fixed and known in advance.

sources.title: World Cup 'Robot Dogs' Put Stadium Security Tech on Display | eWeek
sources.claim: Spot robots were deployed at 2026 World Cup venues (MetLife Stadium, Dallas broadcast centre) for patrols and perimeter inspections, with findings escalated to human security teams; the work is security screening, not playing-surface or equipment compliance.
sources.transferJustification: Same venue type (stadium) but a different task: perimeter security checks and suspicious-package support, with no evidence of surface, goal, net or equipment compliance checks; degree of autonomy during the events is not established.

tasks.label: Signal participants or other officials to make them aware of infractions or to otherwise regulate play or competition.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Court/field team sport (basketball, football, soccer, hockey) at high school through professional level: official blows whistle to stop play, gives the prescribed arm/hand signal for the infraction, indicates direction of possession, and reports the foul number and penalty to the scorer's table or crew chief so it is recorded and understood by players, coaches, and spectators.

Youth and recreational league games (little league, rec soccer, community basketball) with one or two officials: signaling starts and stops of play, indicating scores, cautions, and infractions to young players and parents, often with added verbal explanation so participants understand the call.

instances.label: Youth/high-school soccer, football or basketball official examines participants before and during a game: players line up or are checked during warm-ups while the official looks and feels for shin guards under socks, mouthguards in place, legal cleats, properly fitted helmet/chin strap and required pads, no earrings/necklaces/hair beads, hard casts padded, uniform and undergarment legality. Done on a school field or gym floor with players moving, coaches and spectators present.

Pre-game inspection of loose game equipment at a youth, high-school or college baseball/softball, basketball or volleyball contest: umpire handles each bat to verify the certification stamp/approved-bat sticker, checks for dents, cracks, altered barrels, illegal tape or grip; checks batting helmets for NOCSAE stamp and cracks; inspects catcher's chest protector, mask and shin guards; squeezes/gauges the game balls for inflation and condition. Items are handed to the official at the plate, dugout or scorer's table.

In-situ venue equipment safety check: volleyball referee measures net height and checks antennae, standards and pole padding; soccer referee checks goal anchoring, net attachment and corner flags; basketball official checks rims, backboards and wall/base padding and walks the floor for hazards. Equipment is fixed in place in a school gym or on a field.

Combat-sport or weight-class official examines competitors: wrestling official conducts weigh-ins and skin, fingernail and hair-length checks and inspects headgear; boxing/MMA official watches hand wraps being applied and initials them, inspects gloves, mouthpiece, cup and checks the fighter's body for grease or foreign substances. Performed in a locker room or commission weigh-in room.

Technical inspection in equipment-intensive sports at a dedicated inspection area in the venue: motorsport tech inspection of car body/chassis dimensions, ride height and safety gear in the garage inspection line; track and field call-room weighing and gauging of shots, discuses and javelins; gymnastics apparatus height/tension check before competition.

Professional or Division I game-day equipment compliance inside a stadium or arena: gauging game-ball pressure before the game and at halftime, measuring a hockey stick's curve and length on protest, checking a pitcher's glove color and a catcher's mitt, verifying approved rackets, gloves or bats against the league's approved list. Done by the officiating crew or league equipment inspectors at the bench or in the officials' room.

Mass-start road race, cross-country, triathlon, open-water swim or cycling road race starter: assembles hundreds to thousands of competitors in corrals or on a start line on a public street, park course or open water, checks the course is clear, gives verbal instructions, and starts the wave with a horn or gun under variable weather and crowd conditions.

instances.label: Ballet/classical company dancer learning and drilling a repertory role in the company studio: pointe work, multi-revolution pirouettes, grands jetes, epaulement and partnered pas de deux, refined over weeks of rehearsal under a ballet master's corrections until performance standard.

Modern/contemporary company dancer working a new commission in a rehearsal studio: floor work (rolls, drops, recoveries), off-balance spirals, weight-sharing contact partnering with other dancers, plus repeated marking and full-out runs to internalize phrasing.

Commercial dancer learning a pop/street choreography routine for a concert tour, TV appearance, or music video: choreographer's phone video of the combination, counts to the track, formation changes with other dancers, rehearsed in a rented studio and on the stage until clean and synchronized.

Theme park / cruise ship / casino or corporate-event show performer rehearsing a stylized synchronized production number with costume and hand props on a fixed venue stage, repeating the fixed routine to hit marks and music cues reliably.

Freelance dancer practicing alone at home or in whatever found space is available (living room, garage, park, hotel room), drilling routines and technique learned from video before an audition or gig, on ordinary floors and in limited space.

instances.label: Studio rehearsal or company class: in a dance studio with mirrors and a sprung floor, the dancer learns and drills a new number to counts and music, marking phrases the choreographer demonstrates, repeating passages, adjusting to a live accompanist or a track, and taking corrections between runs.
