Commercial live show in a controlled venue: theme-park stage show or parade, cruise-ship production number, casino revue, arena/halftime spectacle, or backup dancing on a concert tour — a set ensemble routine to a fixed track with formations and costume, repeated several times a day.

Recorded or broadcast work on a soundstage or TV studio: variety special, awards show, commercial, or music video; dancing to playback, hitting marks for camera, repeating the number take after take in sync with the track.

Event, promotional and nightclub dancing inside a venue: trade-show booth or corporate party, club platform or go-go set; largely repetitive, loosely set movement to a live DJ or band, holding the beat through tempo changes for long sets with a crowd close by.

Outdoor found-site work: street festival, parade route, plaza flash mob or community/heritage event; uneven pavement or grass, weather, sun and wind, unbarricaded spectators, sound arriving from a portable PA.

tasks.label: Train, exercise, and attend dance classes to maintain high levels of technical proficiency, physical ability, and physical fitness.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Daily company class at a ballet/modern company studio: the dancer takes a 75–90 minute technique class in which a ballet master gives new barre and center combinations verbally and by marking them, and the dancer must absorb each combination in seconds, execute it with professional line, turnout, balance, jumps and turns, and absorb individual corrections — warming and conditioning the body for the day's rehearsals.

Freelance/commercial dancer takes open classes and workshops at outside studios (jazz, hip-hop, contemporary, tap, heels): fast choreography taught by an instructor, learned and performed in groups across the floor with style and musicality, several times per week to keep skills current and audition-ready.

Cross-training and conditioning at a gym, Pilates studio, or physical-therapy clinic: strength work, cardio, resistance bands, reformer, core and injury-prevention or rehab protocols prescribed by a trainer/PT, performed to build and maintain the dancer's own muscular strength, flexibility, and stamina.

Self-directed warm-up, stretching, and drilling of problem steps in a studio, backstage, or on the stage of a theater before rehearsals and shows — repeating turns, jumps, lifts, or partnering passages until the body is warm and the technical detail is reliable.

Home or on-the-road maintenance training: floor barre, stretching, bodyweight conditioning, and video-guided practice in an apartment living room, hotel room, or park during tour or layoff, in a small improvised space with whatever furniture or props are at hand.

sources.title: China's Walker humanoid robot amazes with precise ballet performance
sources.claim: UBTech's Walker C1 humanoid performed pre-arranged waltz and ballet routines beside human dancers in a staged live demonstration — showing that humanoids can execute prepared choreography, not that they can take a class or condition a body.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing choreography on stage. It does not transfer to this training task: the routine is prepared in advance rather than learned live from an instructor's combinations, and the purpose of class/conditioning — maintaining a human body's strength, flexibility and technique — has no machine analogue.

sources.system: G1 Moves pipeline on Unitree G1
sources.title: Teaching a Robot to Dance | Dell
sources.claim: State-of-the-art humanoid dance comes from an offline pipeline: motion capture or video of a human dancer is retargeted and trained overnight in simulation into a policy the Unitree G1 then replays; the robot does not learn combinations in a class setting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: reproducing dance movement. It shows the acquisition route for robot dance is offline data capture plus overnight RL training, not attending a class and executing an instructor's new combinations on the spot at professional technical quality.

sources.title: Robots learn dance moves to enhance human collaboration | Electronic Specifier
sources.claim: Research whole-body control for humanoid dance imitates upper-body motion while the legs merely track a velocity command, well short of the leg technique (turnout, pointe, jumps, turns, balances) that a dance class demands.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: humanoid imitation of human dance motion. It bounds current capability — expressive upper-body mimicry with simplified leg control — and therefore cannot substantiate executing class combinations at a professional dancer's technical standard.

tasks.label: Coordinate dancing with that of partners or dance ensembles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Performance with a ballet or contemporary company on a theater stage: corps unison work (matching line, spacing, épaulement and musical phrasing with 8-20 other dancers) plus a pas de deux requiring supported pirouettes, promenades and overhead lifts with a human partner, in pointe shoes, to a live orchestra whose tempo varies.

Rehearsal-room work in a dance studio: learning new choreography from the choreographer or dance captain, running it repeatedly with the ensemble, cleaning counts, spacing and dynamics, marking partnering with a specific partner, and absorbing verbal corrections within a rehearsal period of hours to a few days.

Commercial ensemble number performed live or for camera: backup dancing behind a recording artist at an arena concert, on an awards/variety broadcast, or on a music-video set — tight unison choreography, formation changes, hits on the beat, staying synchronized with the artist and the rest of the crew under lights, cues and moving stage elements.

Partner dance with continuous physical contact: ballroom, Latin, swing or tango showcase at a dinner theater, cruise-ship ballroom, competition or corporate event — lead-and-follow through a shared frame, floor craft around other couples, partial improvisation, and lifts or dips executed with a human partner.

Recurring production show in an entertainment venue: theme-park stage show or parade, cruise-ship theater revue, or casino/Vegas-style production — the same ensemble number performed several times a day in costume with a fixed cast, fixed marks and set pieces, close to the audience.

tasks.label: Develop self-understanding of physical capabilities and limitations, and choose dance styles accordingly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Company ballet dancer, in a studio/rehearsal-hall context, takes stock of turnout, extension, foot strength, weight-bearing tolerance and injury history (often with input from the company's physical therapist and ballet master) and decides whether to keep pursuing classical principal repertory or lean toward contemporary/neoclassical work that suits the body better.

Freelance commercial dancer evaluates stamina, joint health, isolations, floorwork tolerance and body type against the demands of audition calls, and decides which style lanes (hip-hop/street, jazz-funk, heels, contemporary) to train in and audition for.

Dancer recovering from injury (e.g., labral tear, stress fracture, ACL) reassesses what the body can now sustain during and after rehab, and shifts style emphasis toward lower-impact or upper-body-centric work such as tap, character, partnering-light, or theatrical movement.

Mid- or late-career dancer notices declining jump height, recovery time, or flexibility across a season, and consciously reweights toward styles and roles with lower athletic demand (character roles, ballroom/social styles, teaching-adjacent performance).

Student or early-career dancer in a conservatory/pre-professional program uses mirror and video self-review, teacher critique, and cross-training results to identify aptitudes and limits (hyperextension, hip mobility, rhythmic facility) and selects a primary style track.

tasks.label: Perform classical, modern, or acrobatic dances in productions, expressing stories, rhythm, and sound with their bodies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Classical ballet / concert-dance repertory performed by a company on a proscenium theater stage: pointe work, partnered lifts and promenades, grands jetés, multiple turns, sustained adagio, in costume, timed to a live orchestra across a two-hour program with wings, marley floor and quick entrances.

Musical theater and production-show dance (Broadway/touring, regional, cruise-ship theaters, theme-park stage shows): jazz, tap and character dance integrated with singing and acting, tight formations with a cast, quick costume changes, scene-to-scene set changes, up to eight shows a week.

Commercial/backup dance for concert tours, TV broadcasts, award shows and music videos: high-energy hip-hop/jazz choreography learned fast at rehearsal, performed in unison with the featured artist, hitting camera marks on an arena stage or studio floor, with props, lifts and floorwork.

Large-scale spectacle/novelty ensemble segment in a televised or arena production: a single set-piece number of synchronized, relatively simple choreography to music (variety-show group number, tech/robot-themed act, parade-style unison routine) where precision timing and uniformity matter more than individual nuance.

Modern/contemporary and experimental concert dance in a theater or black box: floorwork, falls and recoveries, contact-improvisation partnering and weight sharing with other dancers, structured improvisation, and expressive phrasing responding to live music or sound.

Acrobatic and specialty dance plus location work: circus-style tumbling and aerial numbers, breaking/b-boy sets with power moves and floorwork, and gigs at outdoor festivals, parades, street/site-specific performances and private events on found surfaces and improvised stages.

sources.system: KUKA industrial robot arm in 'Huang Yi & KUKA'

tasks.label: Collaborate with choreographers to refine or modify dance steps.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Concert dance company creation rehearsal (ballet/contemporary): in the company's sprung-floor studio, the choreographer sets a new phrase; the dancer executes it full-out and marked, tries alternate arm lines, timings and transitions, reports what does not work with momentum, breath or floor pattern, and offers variations the choreographer accepts or rejects over repeated passes until the phrase is fixed.

Musical theater / Broadway or touring show rehearsal room: the choreographer and dance captain clean a production number; steps are modified to fit costumes, shoes, props, singing while dancing, ensemble spacing and an individual performer's range, with the dancer trying and confirming each change.

Commercial rehearsal for a pop tour, awards show, or music video, in a rented rehearsal studio or soundstage: the choreographer teaches counts and asks dancers to freestyle or style out sections; the dancer contributes personal movement, isolations and texture that the choreographer selects, tweaks and locks into the routine.

On-stage spacing/tech rehearsal or on-set adjustment: in the theater or studio, steps already learned must be modified on the spot for the actual stage size, rake, set pieces, lighting cues, quick changes or camera framing; the dancer runs the change with the choreographer watching from the house or monitor.

Partnering/pas de deux or lift work: the choreographer physically adjusts hand placement, counterbalance and preparation with the dancer and partner, and the dancer feeds back on grip, weight and timing until the lift is safe and reads as intended.

Off-site or nonstandard setting: site-specific and outdoor location work, community-hall or parking-lot rehearsals for a small company, or remote video collaboration where the dancer works out and films requested modifications in a home or found space.

sources.system: Unitree H1 humanoid (Spring Festival Gala Yangge performance)
sources.title: Unitree's bipedal robot shows off slick moves alongside human dancers
sources.claim: The most advanced public humanoid dance performance (16 Unitree H1 robots dancing Yangge alongside human dancers at the 2025 CCTV Spring ...) was a preset routine built from motion-capture data of real dancers, with LiDAR used only for small reactive adjustments — the robots executed a fixed routine rather than contributing to or revising the choreography.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing choreography. It is the closest embodied analogue to this task, but it shows the human-supplied routine being replayed; the creative give-and-take of refining or modifying steps was done entirely by the human choreographers and mocap dancers.

sources.title: Expressive Humanoid — Expressive Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Robots
sources.claim: State-of-the-art expressive humanoid control (ExBody, on a human-sized Unitree H1) learns a whole-body policy that autonomously reproduces dance motions taken from human motion-capture and video in the real world; the movement content originates from human reference motion and the robot has no role in generating or negotiating changes to it.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: executing dance movement autonomously. It bounds what humanoids can do today — track a supplied reference motion in a lab/stage space — and shows no capability to propose, evaluate, or iterate on movement material with a choreographer.

sources.system: Huang Yi & KUKA (KUKA industrial robot arm)
sources.title: Huang Yi & KUKA: A human-robot dance duet | TED Talk
sources.claim: In professional human-robot dance works, the robot is an instrument programmed by the human artist rather than a collaborating dancer: choreographer Huang Yi conceived and programmed the KUKA industrial arm he performs his duet with.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: rehearsing and performing choreography with a choreographer. Transfer fails in the direction that matters: the refinement loop is carried out by the human programming the machine, which is the inverse of the dancer's contribution in this task.

tasks.label: Audition for dance roles or for membership in dance companies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Company audition/open call for a ballet or contemporary company, held in the company's rehearsal studio: the dancer takes a barre and center class taught live by the ballet master, learns and executes combinations (adagio, petit/grand allegro, pirouettes, pointe work) on first showing, in groups, while being observed and progressively cut.

Musical-theater/commercial 'cattle call' in a rented rehearsal studio (e.g., Equity chorus call): dancer signs in, learns a 60-90 second jazz/theater combination taught in 15-25 minutes, performs it in groups of four to six with correct spacing, style and facing, and may also sing 16 bars.

Callback or role-specific audition on a theater stage with the choreographer present: learn an excerpt of the actual repertory, take live corrections and adjustments, partner with another dancer (lifts, promenades), and perform in costume/character under stage lighting.

Commercial dance audition (music video, artist tour, backup dancing) in a rented dance studio: hip-hop/street/heels combination taught fast, plus a freestyle/improvisation round and a personality/look assessment in front of choreographer and client.

Self-tape/video audition: dancer records a prescribed combination or a reel of technique and improvisation, alone in a home living room, garage, park or borrowed studio space, framing and lighting the shot themselves, then edits and submits it.

Specialty entertainment audition (cruise line, theme park, Las Vegas revue, professional dance team) held in a hotel ballroom or convention space: multiple styles taught back-to-back, height/measurement and costume-fit check, tricks/tumbling or tap section, and a short interview.

sources.title: Korean humanoid robot learns viral K-POP dance from smartphone videos
sources.claim: A humanoid robot (ROBOTIS AI Sapiens) learned a viral K-pop dance motion from ordinary smartphone video via motion retargeting and simulation reinforcement learning, then executed it autonomously in a lab demonstration; the pipeline is offline (video capture, retargeting, sim training, sim2real) rather than learning a combination live in a studio, and covers a single rehearsed routine, not professional-level technique across styles.
sources.transferJustification: Closest related task: reproducing a human dance routine. It does not transfer to auditioning, because the routine is learned offline over a training pipeline rather than taught live in the room, and the output is a single rehearsed motion rather than evaluated professional technique.

sources.title: Humanoid robot dance crew capture spotlight on America's Got Talent
sources.claim: Eight Unitree G1 humanoids performed a synchronized dance routine alongside a human dancer in an America's Got Talent audition; the routine was pre-choreographed and the method of control was not disclosed (observers on set speculated how the machines were being controlled), so autonomy cannot be established.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing a dance routine at a televised talent-show audition. It does not substantiate this task because control autonomy is unestablished and the act is a fixed pre-produced novelty routine, not learning and executing choreography given on the spot for casting in a dance role.

sources.system: Boston Dynamics Atlas / Spot with Choreographer software
sources.title: How Boston Dynamics' robots learned to dance
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' widely circulated Atlas/Spot dance videos were produced with Choreographer software in which pre-programmed movements are dragged and tuned on a timeline, i.e., authored scripted routines rather than robots learning or improvising dance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot dance performance. Shows state-of-the-art robot dancing is hand-authored offline, which cannot supply the on-the-spot learning, correction-taking and evaluated technique an audition requires.

tasks.label: Attend costume fittings, photography sessions, and makeup calls associated with dance performances.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Costume fitting in a ballet/modern company's wardrobe shop: the dancer strips to tights, is measured, tries on tutus, unitards, headpieces and shoes, holds still while the cutter pins and marks, then executes port de bras, développés, jumps and partnering lifts to test range of motion, reporting where the garment binds, gaps or catches. The costume is fitted to that dancer's body for the roles they will dance.

Makeup and hair call in the company dressing room before a performance or dress rehearsal: the dancer arrives on schedule, sits at the station while stage makeup, false lashes, wigs and hairpieces are applied and pinned (or applies their own to the designer's plot), sits still for touch-ups, and leaves with their own face and hair ready for the stage under lights.

Publicity/promotional photography session in a photo studio or theater lobby: the dancer, in costume and makeup, repeats jumps, holds arabesques, penchés and lifts on the photographer's cue for one to three hours, adjusts angle and line to lighting and direction, and the resulting images of that dancer are used in season marketing.

Photo call / press shoot on stage during dress rehearsal: the dancer performs excerpts of the choreography in full costume under performance lighting while photographers and video crews shoot, then holds marked positions on request; quick-change and costume-check adjustments happen in the wings between excerpts.

Film, television, commercial or music-video work: fittings at a rental costume house or on a location trailer, makeup in a trailer or on set, and posing/dancing for stills on location (street, park, warehouse) with variable weather, crowds and non-standard layout.

sources.developer: Hong Kong Polytechnic University (Institute of Textiles and Clothing)
sources.title: i.Dummy : Robotic Mannequin for Fashion Design and Fitting — PolyU Knowledge Transfer
sources.claim: A robotic shape-changing mannequin (i.Dummy) can automatically adopt specified body shapes and dimensions for garment design and fitting, but it is a design tool used by human designers, not a substitute for a performer attending a fitting of their own costume.
sources.transferJustification: Closest adjacent system to a costume fitting. It does not transfer: the accepted output of a dancer's fitting is a costume tailored to that specific dancer's body and validated by the dancer moving through choreography, which a programmable dress form cannot deliver.

sources.title: Robotics Meets Runway: Unitree G1's Catwalk Debut at SHFW
sources.claim: Humanoid robots have appeared on fashion runways and in staged shows alongside human models, but the appearances are choreographed showcase walks, with autonomy of the presentation not established.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: a humanoid presenting garments/posing in front of cameras. It does not transfer: the dancer's photo call and fitting produce images and costumes of and for a specific human performer cast in the production; a robot's runway walk cannot yield that output, and autonomy is unclear.

sources.title: World's 1st lipstick with robotic arm brings hands-free makeup to all
sources.claim: Robotic systems can apply cosmetics to a human face (e.g., a hands-free robotic lipstick applicator using computer vision), i.e., they can occupy the makeup-artist side of a makeup call, not the performer's side.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: cosmetic application by machine. It does not transfer: at a makeup call the dancer is the person being made up; the accepted output is the dancer's own face prepared for the stage, so no robot can perform the dancer's side of the appointment.

tasks.label: Monitor the field of dance to remain aware of current trends and innovations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Company dancer watches recorded and streamed performances online (company channels, festival streams, social platforms such as Instagram/TikTok) at home or backstage to keep up with choreographic trends, new works, and viral movement styles.
Dancer attends live performances by other companies, showcases, or student/competition events as an audience member, observing repertoire, staging, and stylistic innovation.
Dancer takes open classes, workshops, or masterclasses with visiting teachers/choreographers to absorb emerging techniques and vocabulary, and to see what other dancers in the field are doing.

Dancer reads trade press, reviews, newsletters, casting notices, and social media posts, and follows choreographers, companies, and competitions to track who is making what and what is being programmed.
Dancer talks with peers, agents, teachers, and choreographers at auditions, conventions, or conferences to exchange information about trends, styles in demand, and innovations in the field.

tasks.label: Prepare pointe shoes, by sewing or other means, for use in rehearsals and performance.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Sewing ribbons and elastics onto a new pair of pointe shoes at home or in a company dressing room: the dancer folds the heel to find the ribbon angle, marks the cotton lining, folds and singes ribbon ends, then hand-stitches a square of whip/running stitches with waxed thread or dental floss through the lining and side wall but not through the outer satin, avoiding the drawstring, knotting off each of six or more attachments per pair.

Breaking in and customizing the shoe body before use: bending and softening the shank by hand at the dancer's own arch point, crushing or hammering the box against a floor or door frame, stepping on the shoe, sometimes cutting or shortening the shank to three-quarter length and pulling the nails, with acceptance judged by how the shoe feels on the dancer's foot.

Darning the platform: hand-stitching a thick border of yarn or floss around the edge of the toe platform of each shoe with a needle, to widen and stabilize the standing surface and slow wear; freehand needlework on the curved tip of a finished shoe, done at home or in a studio.

Preparing the outer surfaces for traction and wear: cutting or sanding the satin off the platform tip, scratching or scoring the leather outsole with a knife, rasp or sandpaper, and roughing the shank sole so the shoe grips the stage floor.

Applying hardeners and adhesives: pouring or brushing shellac, floor sealer or cyanoacrylate 'jet glue' into the toe box and along the shank of each shoe to stiffen soft spots and extend shoe life, plus gluing in toe pads or spacers, then setting the shoes aside to dry.

Quick preparation and repairs during a rehearsal block or performance run, in a theater dressing room or backstage: re-sewing a ribbon that has pulled loose, replacing a stretched elastic, re-darning a worn platform, rotating and drying several pairs, and labeling pairs for particular acts, under time pressure between calls.

sources.system: Robot-based shoe manufacturing automation system (industrial manipulators with roughing and cementing tools, 3-D scanner)
sources.developer: Korea Institute of Industrial Technology / academic team (published in Machines, MDPI)
sources.title: Robot-Based Automation for Upper and Sole Manufacturing in Shoe Production
sources.claim: Industrial robot manipulators with a digitizer and 3-D scanning perform roughing of shoe uppers and cementing (adhesive application) on lasted shoes and soles along automatically generated tool paths in an automated production testbed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic roughing/abrading and adhesive application on a fixtured finished shoe. It carries over to scoring soles, sanding satin off the platform, and applying shellac/jet glue to a pointe shoe: same class of object (a lasted shoe held in a fixture), same operation (tool follows a scanned 3-D path over the shoe surface), and comparable precision requirements.

sources.system: Stäubli RX90 robot cells for cementing and roughing
sources.developer: Stäubli (integrated at Brightwood, Florida shoe manufacturer)
sources.title: Robotics in footwear manufacturing is old news. Here's why: | Solereview
sources.claim: Commercial footwear plants have long run industrial robot cells that perform cementing and roughing on lasted shoes at production rates.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: production roughing and glue application on finished shoes inside a fenced factory cell. It substantiates that abrading defined regions of a shoe surface and depositing adhesive along a shoe's contour are done by machines at accepted production quality, which is what sole-scoring and hardener application on a pointe shoe require.

sources.system: Sewbo/Siemens robotic sewing system (ARM Institute project, RACER microfactory)
sources.title: Project Highlight: Advancing Automated Robotic Sewing - ARM Institute
sources.claim: A robotic sewing system moves flat fabric panels through industrial sewing machines to produce garment seams, matured from prototype to industrial hardware (TRL 8-9) in a containerized microfactory; it sews only flat panels fed to a sewing machine, not finished three-dimensional articles.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated sewing of textiles. Transfer to pointe-shoe ribbon sewing fails: the system handles flat panels presented to a stationary sewing machine head, whereas ribbons and elastics must be hand-stitched onto the inside wall of a stiffened, closed three-dimensional shoe without piercing the outer satin.

sources.system: Robotic sewing and knot-tying system for stent graft manufacturing
sources.title: Robotic Sewing and Knot Tying for Personalized Stent Graft Manufacturing (arXiv 1803.08478)
sources.claim: A customized robotic sewing device with closed-loop visual servoing sews a three-dimensional structured object (a personalized stent graft mounted in a lab rig) with sub-millimetre stitch accuracy and performs automatic knot tying.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: needle-and-thread stitching with knot tying on a fixtured 3-D object. Objects differ materially: an open fabric tube on a mandrel with two-sided needle access versus the confined interior of a stiffened satin pointe shoe where the stitch must catch the lining only and miss the drawstring, so completion of the shoe instance is not substantiated.

sources.system: TARS T-/A-Series humanoid with AWE 2.0 model
sources.title: TARS Demonstrates a Robot That Can Perform Hand Embroidery, Breaking Through a Key Automation Bottleneck in Flexible Manufacturing
sources.claim: A humanoid robot publicly performed hand embroidery at a live event, threading a needle and stitching ... bimanually with sub-millimetre precision; the report does not state whether execution was autonomous or teleoperated.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: freehand needle-and-thread stitching of flexible material, the closest public analogue to sewing ribbons or darning a platform. Autonomy is not established in the source, so per the rating rules it is treated as teleoperated and cannot support a positive judgment.

tasks.label: Perform in productions, singing or acting in addition to dancing, if required.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Musical theater production (Broadway, national tour, regional or dinner theater): ensemble dancer performs eight shows a week on a set stage, singing chorus vocals live while dancing, playing small character/acting roles, doing partnered lifts, quick costume changes and prop work.

Concert dance company production (ballet, modern, contemporary): technically demanding repertory in a proscenium theater — pointe work, grand allegro, partnered lifts, floor work — with dramatic characterization or mime rather than speech, performed to live or recorded music with company-standard artistry.

Theme park, cruise ship or casino revue: costumed production numbers repeated three to five times daily on a fixed show stage or parade route, with lip-synced vocals, scripted character patter and direct guest interaction, in heavy character costume and heat.

Backup dancing for a recording artist in a live concert, televised gala, awards show or variety broadcast: unison choreography beside the artist on an arena or studio stage, synced to music and lighting cues; no live singing or spoken role required.

Music video, film, or commercial shoot: dancing to playback on a soundstage or location set across many takes, with camera-specific blocking, choreography adjusted on the day by the choreographer/director, styling and costume, and screen-level expressiveness.

Corporate event, trade show, festival or variety-competition act: a short choreographed routine on a temporary stage or ballroom floor, purely dance, no singing or acting, rehearsed in advance and performed once or a few times for a booked client.

sources.claim: Disney's Stuntronics figure is an autonomous aerial performing robot used as a Spider-Man stunt double in the Avengers Campus theme-park show.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing a scripted beat in a theme-park show. Transfer fails for the revue instance — it is a single launched aerial stunt, not costumed character dance choreography with lip-sync and guest interaction.

sources.title: Video Friday: This Japanese Robot Can Conduct a Human Orchestra and Sing Opera - IEEE Spectrum
sources.claim: The android Alter 3 both conducts a human orchestra and sings in the staged production 'Scary Beauty', showing machine vocal performance in a theatrical production.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: singing/acting in a staged production. Transfer fails here because Alter 3 is a fixed upper-body android that cannot dance, so it cannot cover the combined sing-while-dancing instances.

tasks.label: Teach dance students.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Recreational/pre-competitive class for children and teens at a private dance studio (ballet, jazz, tap, hip-hop): 12-25 students on a sprung floor with mirrors and barres; the dancer demonstrates full-body steps and combinations, cues to music, watches the room, gives individual verbal and hands-on alignment corrections, manages behavior and safety, and builds recital choreography over a term.

Adult recreational class at a studio, gym, or community-center room (ballroom/salsa, contemporary, adult ballet, dance-fitness): mixed ability and ages, partner rotations, teacher demonstrates from the front and mirrored, breaks steps down, re-teaches on the fly for people who cannot follow, and adjusts holds and frames by hand.

Private or semi-private lesson at the studio: one or two students, a full 30-60 minute session tailored to level and goals (technique fix, competition routine, audition prep), including physical partnering, spotting turns and lifts, and hands-on correction of the student's body position.

Company class, university/conservatory class, or guest master class for pre-professional dancers: the dancer marks and demonstrates long, novel combinations at speed, sets choreography on the cast, gives precise stylistic and technical corrections to advanced bodies, and answers artistic questions.

Teaching outside a dance facility: school gym or cafeteria outreach residency, community hall, church basement, a client's living room for wedding first-dance coaching, or a pop-up/outdoor workshop; floor, mirrors, sound, space and student group vary site to site and are not kept to any standard.

sources.system: Male-type Dance Partner Robot (PBDR-derived dance teaching robot)
sources.developer: Tohoku University (Kosuge Lab; Paez Granados et al.)
sources.title: Dance Teaching by a Robot: Combining Cognitive and Physical Human-Robot Interaction for Supporting the Skill Learning Process
sources.claim: A wheeled dance-partner robot at Tohoku University acted as a waltz teacher, physically guiding a novice through a basic figure and giving performance feedback; the platform has no feet, so a human dancer had to demonstrate the footwork to the students first.
sources.transferJustification: This is the closest published attempt at the task itself (teaching a dance student). It is cited to show the ceiling: a lab study, one basic waltz figure, a footless wheeled body that cannot demonstrate steps, with a human dancer supplying the demonstration.

sources.system: Unitree G1 humanoid (eight units, America's Got Talent season 21 audition)
sources.title: Humanoid robot dance crew capture spotlight on America's Got Talent
sources.claim: Humanoid robots can execute demanding pre-set dance choreography on stage in sync with a human dancer, including flips, but the routines are fixed programs; there is no reported observation of students or corrective instruction.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing choreography, i.e. the demonstration half of dance teaching. Transfer is limited: the choreography is authored offline and replayed, so it does not show a robot generating, breaking down, or adapting material for learners.

sources.system: R-COOL humanoid robot coach (from the KERAAL robot-coach line of work)
sources.developer: IMT Atlantique / CHRU Brest / Generation Robots consortium
sources.title: Technical Feasibility of Supervision of Stretching Exercises by a Humanoid Robot Coach for Chronic Low Back Pain: The R-COOL Randomized Trial
sources.claim: In a randomized feasibility trial in rehabilitation centers, a humanoid robot coach supervised 30-minute stretching sessions for chronic low-back-pain patients, using camera-based movement analysis to deliver prerecorded corrective feedback, versus a physiotherapist control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: instructing a human in body movement with corrective feedback inside an institutional facility. Transfer is partial only: the repertoire is a handful of pre-authored stretches with scripted messages, not novel full-body choreography demonstrated, taught and corrected to an employer's standard.

sources.title: Robots making inroads in Japan's elder care facilities, but costs still high
sources.claim: Pepper humanoids have been deployed in Japanese eldercare facilities to lead group exercise/recreation sessions in front of residents, running set routines rather than assessing or correcting individual participants.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: leading a group through movement in a structured facility. Transfer fails for dance teaching: Pepper has a wheeled base and no legs, plays fixed routines, and does not demonstrate footwork, correct technique, or set choreography.

sources.developer: PAL Robotics platform; university research team (arXiv 2408.05301)
sources.title: Dancing with REEM-C: A robot-to-human physical-social communication study
sources.claim: A study of a full-size humanoid waltzing with a human found that current humanoid hardware supports only hand-force exchange and slow, simple footwork, requiring an open position instead of the normal closed ballroom hold.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: partnered social dance with a human, the physical core of ballroom/partner instruction. It establishes the state-of-the-art ceiling for a robot dancing with a student and shows worker-quality partnering and hands-on correction are out of reach.

tasks.label: Devise and choreograph dance for self or others.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Company or freelance dancer devises a short solo/variation for themselves in a rehearsal studio — selecting movement vocabulary, phrasing, musical counts, and spatial pathways, then fixing the sequence so it can be repeated and performed later.

Commercial choreographer-dancer creates a routine for a music video, TV segment, or artist tour: builds 8-counts to a track, sets formations and camera-facing angles, and delivers the set piece to backup dancers and the director within a tight deadline.

Studio/school dance teacher choreographs a recital or competition piece for a group of students, tailoring difficulty to the dancers' skill levels, the stage size, costumes, and competition rules, and revising the sequence over several weeks of rehearsals.

Concert/theater dancer contributes devised material or choreographs a section for a staged production (ballet, modern, musical), collaborating with a director/composer, adapting movement to set, lighting cues, and other performers' entrances.

Event or community gig: choreographing a wedding first dance, corporate/flash-mob number, cheer or drill-team routine, or a social-media dance for non-professional participants, with the sequence set to their abilities and the venue's space.

roles.title: Choreographers
roles.description: Create new dance routines. Rehearse performance of routines. May direct and stage presentations.
roles.sector: Arts, design, entertainment, sports, and media

tasks.label: Direct rehearsals to instruct dancers in dance steps and in techniques to achieve desired effects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Studio rehearsal with a concert dance or ballet company: the choreographer runs the cast through repertory phrases, counts music, gives verbal corrections on timing, line, dynamics and intent, and marks or demonstrates phrases to convey the desired effect until the section is performance-ready.

Commercial rehearsal (music video, tour, awards show, TV) in a rented studio: the choreographer and assistants teach a combination quickly to professional backup dancers, clean formations and levels, and adjust the material to the artist and camera in a few sessions.

Musical theater, school, or community production rehearsal: the choreographer teaches staging and steps to performers with mixed dance training, simplifies material to ability, coordinates with the stage director and music director, and repeats instruction over many weeks.

Competition or studio-school team rehearsal with youth dancers: the choreographer/teacher drills technique (turns, leaps, synchronization), gives individual corrections and occasional hands-on placement cues, and manages the group's focus and pacing.

On-site spacing/technical rehearsal on a stage or film set: the choreographer adapts previously taught material to the actual floor, sightlines, lighting, cameras and costumes, calling adjustments to dancers and coordinating with production staff under time pressure.

tasks.label: Advise dancers on standing and moving properly, teaching correct dance techniques to help prevent injuries.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Professional company rehearsal studio: during a run-through, the choreographer watches dancers and gives verbal notes and demonstrations on alignment, turnout, weight placement, and safe landings so dancers avoid strain over a long rehearsal period.

Dance school or conservatory class: the choreographer/teacher explains and models correct technique (plié depth, spotting, spinal alignment) to a group of students, occasionally using light hands-on tactile cues to indicate where a body part should be.

One-on-one coaching of a dancer who is returning from or prone to injury: reviewing the dancer's habitual movement patterns, advising modifications to the choreography, and coordinating advice with a physical therapist or athletic trainer.

Commercial set (music video, TV, live show) or theater stage: quick technique and safety notes between takes on a raked, slick, or cramped surface, including warm-up guidance and advice on pacing repeated high-impact movements.

Amateur or community setting (cheer squad, community theater, dance-fitness class, school musical) with untrained bodies: instructing participants on basic posture, safe lifting/partnering, and how to stop or modify a movement that hurts.

tasks.label: Teach students, dancers, and other performers about rhythm and interpretive movement.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Studio technique or repertory class: the choreographer teaches student dancers to hear and hold a rhythm — counting phrases aloud, clapping or drumming counts, demonstrating steps to music, then correcting individuals' timing and musicality verbally and by re-demonstration.

Rehearsal with a professional company or cast: the choreographer explains and demonstrates the interpretive intent behind a phrase (dynamics, breath, character, emotional quality), gives imagery and notes, and coaches dancers until the movement quality reads as intended.

Coaching non-dancer performers (actors, singers, skaters, cheer or drill members, models) in basic musicality and expressive movement for a specific production, using simplified counts, walk-throughs, and repeated verbal notes.

Community, youth, school, or recreational settings — a competition team, K-12 program, or community workshop — where the choreographer teaches beginners rhythm fundamentals and improvisation/interpretive exercises to mixed-ability groups.
Remote or mediated instruction: teaching rhythm and interpretive movement over video conference, in a filmed masterclass, or via recorded notes and annotated video sent to dancers.

tasks.label: Record dance movements and their technical aspects, using a technical understanding of the patterns and formations of choreography.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Direct and stage dance presentations for various forms of entertainment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Staging dance numbers for a musical theater production: in a rehearsal hall and then on the theater stage, the choreographer sets blocking and formations for a cast, adjusts spacing to the set, coordinates entrances/exits with the stage director and stage manager, and gives verbal/visual notes through spacing and tech rehearsals until the number reads as intended from the house.

Directing and staging a concert-dance or ballet company program: the choreographer stages the work on company dancers in a studio and theater, decides ordering and transitions between sections, coordinates with lighting/costume designers and the artistic director, and gives corrections in dress and tech rehearsals.

Staging dance for a studio recital or competition team: the choreographer arranges entrances, formations, and levels for groups of students of mixed ability, cues counts and music, adapts staging to the rented venue's stage size and wings, and runs the spacing/dress rehearsal.

Staging dance for camera on a film, TV, commercial, or music-video shoot: the choreographer sets performers' marks and movement to the camera frame and lens, coordinates with the director and DP over takes and coverage, adjusts the staging between setups, and gives performance notes on set.

Staging dance for live commercial entertainment — cruise-ship production shows, theme-park shows, halftime/arena shows, awards shows, or corporate events: the choreographer adapts a routine to the venue's stage, field, or floor, sets formations relative to cameras and audience sightlines, coordinates cues with technical staff, and runs the on-site rehearsal.

tasks.label: Choose the music, sound effects, or spoken narrative to accompany a dance.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Experiment with different types of dancers, steps, dances, and placements, testing ideas informally to get feedback from dancers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Contemporary/concert dance company creation session in a rehearsal studio: the choreographer proposes movement material and variations, tries different dancers on the same phrase, asks how a transition feels in the body, and revises based on the dancers' informal reactions. Output is a revised movement idea, not a changed physical object.

Musical theatre or commercial stage rehearsal on a taped/marked studio floor: the choreographer tests formations, spacing and entrances/exits with a group and the dance captain, runs the option against music, and solicits quick feedback about sightlines, breath and traffic before settling on a version.

Casting/typing experimentation: trying the same step or phrase on different dancers (heights, techniques, partnering pairings) in an audition room or studio to see which body and quality suits which role, gathering the dancers' informal comments on fit and difficulty.

Solo or one-on-one studio exploration: the choreographer improvises alone or with a single dancer, films takes on a phone, reviews the footage, and sends clips to collaborators or dancers for informal reactions before bringing the idea to the full cast.

Screen/field work (music video shoot, TV/soundstage, gym, cheer or competition floor, school auditorium): placements and steps are tested against camera angles or a non-standard performing space, with informal feedback from dancers about footing, spacing and visibility.

tasks.label: Seek influences from other art forms, such as theatre, the visual arts, and architecture.

tasks.label: Develop ideas for creating dances, keeping notes and sketches to record influences.

instances.label: Concert/contemporary choreographer developing the concept for a new work: listening to scores, reading source texts, watching archival video, and journaling written notes and rough movement sketches over weeks, mostly at home or in a studio office.

Studio ideation session: the choreographer improvises or marks movement alone or with one dancer to test ideas, then records counts, images, phrase names and stick-figure sketches in a notebook or phone notes app.
Commercial choreographer (music video, artist tour, TV) assembling visual and music references into a mood board and writing concept notes and formation sketches for a client or director brief.
Dance-school or competition choreographer planning routines for a known group of students: noting counts, sections, skill placements and floor patterns in a planning notebook before rehearsals begin.
Musical theater or opera choreographer researching period/social dance style and meeting the director, then sketching staging diagrams and traffic patterns on paper or in plotting software.

tasks.label: Coordinate production music with music directors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Design dances for individual dancers, dance companies, musical theatre, opera, fashion shows, film, television productions, and special events, and for dancers ranging from beginners to professionals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Concert-dance commission: choreographer devises an original work for a professional company in a rented studio, generating movement phrases to a score, structuring sections, spacing groups, and delivering the finished movement design to the dancers and rehearsal director.

Musical theatre staging: choreographer designs production numbers for a regional, school, or touring musical, fitting movement to the book, score, set, and the mixed skill levels of the cast, and handing the designed numbers to the director and dance captain.

Recreational/competition studio work: choreographer creates routines for classes and competition teams of children and teens ranging from beginners to pre-professionals, tailoring difficulty, formations, and music cuts to each group.

Commercial screen and runway work: choreographer designs movement for a music video, TV number, film sequence, or fashion show, shaping the movement to camera angles, edits, runway geometry, and costume constraints, in consultation with the director or creative team.

Special events and opera: choreographer designs movement for a corporate event, halftime/parade show, awards number, or opera chorus staging, working to a client brief, venue plan, and non-dancer or semi-professional performers.

tasks.label: Audition performers for one or more dance parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Open-call or agency audition for a musical theater production, held in a rented dance studio or on a theater stage: the choreographer (or an assistant) sets a short combination, dancers perform in groups of 4-8, the choreographer watches, keeps notes on numbered dancers, makes cuts, and confers with the director and music director on who advances to callbacks and who is cast.

Company audition for a concert dance company or ballet/contemporary project in the company's home studio: dozens of pre-screened dancers take a class-style barre and center, then learn repertory excerpts; the choreographer evaluates technique, musicality, partnering, and stylistic fit over several hours and selects dancers or apprentices.

Commercial audition for a music video, TV/awards show, tour, theme park, or cruise-line contract: dancers submitted by agents learn a fast, style-specific combination, often perform to camera or 'freestyle', and the choreographer evaluates on-camera presence and look alongside a client/producer, then submits a shortlist.

Remote review of self-tape or video submissions: the choreographer watches submitted reels or a taught-combination video filmed by the dancer, scores or ranks candidates against role requirements, and shortlists people for a live callback — no in-person session at all.

Small-scale audition for a school, university, regional, competition-team, or community production, held in a school gym, church hall, or studio: a mixed-ability group learns a simple combination, the choreographer assesses skill level and places dancers into parts or ensemble tracks, often also handling paperwork and parent/participant communication.

tasks.label: Assess students' dancing abilities to determine where improvement or change is needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In a dance studio, the choreographer watches a class or company group run a combination repeatedly, tracking alignment, timing, spacing, and musicality across many bodies at once, and forms a judgment about which dancers need what corrections.

At an audition or casting call, the choreographer evaluates candidates performing taught phrases and improvisation, ranking technical ability, retention speed, and stylistic fit to determine suitability and developmental gaps.

In a private coaching or small-group session, the choreographer assesses one dancer in detail — turnout, extension, weight transfer, breath, phrasing — to diagnose specific limitations and set improvement priorities.

Away from the studio, the choreographer reviews video recordings of rehearsals or performances, pausing and replaying to identify technical and expressive shortcomings and to prepare notes for the dancers.

During a stage run-through of a production, the choreographer watches from the house under performance lighting and costume conditions, judging ensemble cohesion, spacing, and individual execution to determine what must change before opening.

tasks.label: Design sets, lighting, costumes, and other artistic elements of productions, in collaboration with cast members.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Train, exercise, and attend dance classes to maintain high levels of technical proficiency, physical ability, and physical fitness.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Choreographer takes an open technique class (ballet, jazz, modern, hip-hop, tap) at a commercial dance studio: sprung floor, barres, mirrors; an instructor gives new combinations verbally and by demonstration, the worker executes them across the floor with a group and absorbs individual corrections, sustaining professional-level turnout, extension, turns and jumps.

Solo technique maintenance in the rehearsal studio or theater the choreographer already works in: personal warm-up, floor barre, stretching, drilling pirouettes/jumps and movement vocabulary before or after rehearsing a company, keeping the body able to demonstrate phrases full-out to dancers.

Cross-training and conditioning at a gym, Pilates studio or physical-therapy clinic: weights, cardio, core and mobility work, injury-prevention and rehab protocols prescribed after strain, performed on standard equipment under a trainer's or therapist's supervision.

Home-based training: floor stretching, conditioning and technique practice in a living room, basement or garage with limited space and no mirror or barre; also drilling unfamiliar styles learned from video to keep vocabulary current.

Workshops, masterclasses and intensives away from the home studio — convention ballrooms, guest studios, festival or outdoor rehearsal spaces with unfamiliar floors and layouts — where the worker learns and executes another teacher's material at speed.

sources.title: China's Walker humanoid robot amazes with precise ballet performance
sources.claim: UBTECH's Walker C1 full-size humanoid performed Swan Lake ballet and waltz movements alongside human dancers in a staged live demonstration; the report describes balance and motion-control quality but gives no indication the robot learned the choreography itself or trained to acquire it.
sources.transferJustification: Closest available analogue to dance-class execution: a humanoid producing ballet-style movement. It does not substantiate the task, because the demonstration is a pre-authored stage routine with unstated autonomy, not learning combinations from an instructor or maintaining a body's fitness.

sources.title: Unitree Robotics teaches humanoids to dance with motion capture data
sources.claim: Unitree's H1, H1-2 and G1 humanoid dance sequences are produced by retargeting the LAFAN1 human motion-capture dataset onto the robots, i.e. replaying pre-recorded human motion under kinematic constraints, rather than learning movement in a class setting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is robot dance performance. It shows the state of the art is replay of captured human motion on a stage or lab floor, which does not transfer to attending a class, taking corrections, or building and maintaining human physical capacity.

sources.system: Deep Fourier Mimic (DFM) on a legged entertainment robot
sources.developer: ETH Zurich Robotic Systems Lab (Watanabe, Li, Hutter)
sources.title: DFM: Deep Fourier Mimic for Expressive Dance Motion Learning
sources.claim: Research on expressive robot dance (Deep Fourier Mimic, ICRA 2025) learns policies that track artist-authored or captured reference dance motions on a legged robot in the lab; the choreography itself still originates from humans and the work targets entertainment motion, not physical training.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is autonomous execution of dance motion. Even the autonomous case reproduces reference choreography in a controlled lab, so it cannot stand in for a choreographer attending class to acquire and maintain personal technical proficiency and fitness.

tasks.label: Read and study story lines and musical scores to determine how to translate ideas and moods into dance movements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Musical theater choreographer reads the libretto/script and studies the piano-vocal score for a book musical, identifying song structure, character intentions, tempo and mood shifts, and deciding what dance vocabulary and staging ideas each number calls for before rehearsals begin.

Commercial, music-video, or competition choreographer studies a recorded track repeatedly: counting phrases, mapping lyrics, accents, breaks and dynamics, and deciding the movement quality, texture and mood the piece should convey.

Narrative concert-dance or ballet choreographer studies a full orchestral score together with a literary source or scenario, deriving movement motifs for characters and shaping the mood arc of each scene.

Studio, school-recital, drill team, or cheer choreographer selects and analyzes music and a theme, reviewing lyrics and musical structure to plan movement appropriate to the performers' skill level and the program's mood.

Film/TV or industrial-show choreographer reads screenplay scene descriptions and director notes alongside temp or final music tracks to determine how the required ideas and moods should be expressed in camera-aware movement.

tasks.label: Restage traditional dances and works in dance companies' repertoires, developing new interpretations.

instances.label: Classical ballet company (regional or major) restages a standard-repertory story ballet such as Swan Lake or The Nutcracker: the regisseur/choreographer reconstructs the work from memory, archival video, and notation, decides cuts, casting, and interpretive changes, then teaches and coaches corps and principals in the studio and refines the staging in theater rehearsals.

Modern/contemporary company revives a licensed repertory work from an estate or foundation (e.g., Graham, Limon, Ailey, Balanchine Trust): an approved repetiteur transmits the choreography from archival film plus embodied memory, adjusts it to the current dancers, and sets the interpretive intent through coaching notes.

University, pre-professional, or civic company restages a public-domain or traditional work with a smaller and less experienced cast: the choreographer adapts the original for fewer dancers, a smaller stage, and reduced technical demands, developing a new reading of the piece and rehearsing it over several weeks.

Folkloric or culturally traditional dance (e.g., ballet folklorico, Bharatanatyam, flamenco, Native or diasporic forms) restaged for a company or festival program: the choreographer works with tradition bearers and community sources, reorders and theatricalizes material for the proscenium, and rehearses the ensemble.

Commercial or musical-theatre restaging: the associate choreographer/dance supervisor reproduces an existing production's numbers for a new cast, tour, or regional licensee, adapting spacing to a different stage and re-teaching the material during a compressed rehearsal period.

tasks.label: Use gestures to shape the music being played, communicating desired tempo, phrasing, tone, color, pitch, volume, and other performance aspects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Professional or community orchestra rehearsal and concert: conductor stands on a podium and uses baton beat patterns, left-hand shaping, cueing, and eye contact to communicate tempo, dynamics, balance, and phrasing to ~40-90 players reading the same score in real time.

Choral conducting (church choir, community chorus, school chorus): director faces singers and uses hand and arm gestures, breath cues, and facial expression to indicate entrances, releases, vowel color, blend, and dynamic shaping during weekly rehearsals and services/concerts.

School band/orchestra director in a rehearsal room: conducts developing student players, gesturing beat and style while simultaneously diagnosing errors, exaggerating gestures for pedagogical clarity, and adapting the gesture to what the students actually produce.

Musical theater pit, opera, or worship-service conducting: director gestures to coordinate an instrumental ensemble with singers/actors on stage, following and correcting live tempo drift, cutoffs, and vamps that depend on stage action.

Recording/film-scoring session or small chamber ensemble led from the instrument: conductor gestures (often to click/picture or from the keyboard) to signal tempo changes, entrances, and expressive shaping for a small group of players under time pressure.

Community, civic, or regional orchestra/band conductor runs evening rehearsals with amateur and semi-professional players in a rehearsal hall and conducts the public concert in a local auditorium, adjusting tempo and dynamics in real time to the players' responses.

Professional conductor or music director leads a professional orchestra, opera, or musical-theater pit ensemble: rehearsals in the hall or theater, coordination with soloists and staging, and live performance conducting where the ensemble follows the beat pattern, cues, and expressive gestures.

Studio/recording session conductor directs an orchestra or vocal ensemble for a film score, album, or jingle date, conducting to click track or picture, communicating with the booth, and re-taking passages to achieve the producer's desired balance and phrasing.

tasks.label: Perform before live audiences in concerts, recitals, educational presentations, and other social gatherings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Ensemble concert in a concert hall, theater, or pit: symphony/chamber orchestra, chorus, big band or musical-theater pit player performs a full printed program before a ticketed audience, reading scores, following a conductor's beat and cues, tuning, blending and balancing with the section, and adjusting dynamics and phrasing live.

Amplified gig at a bar, club, brewery, or restaurant: solo singer-guitarist/keyboardist or 3-5 piece band loads in, sound-checks, and plays two to three 45-minute sets of covers and originals, takes audience requests, banters between songs, and adapts the set to the room's energy.

Private social event: wedding ceremony/reception, private party, or corporate function in a hotel ballroom, banquet tent, backyard, or private home; the musician plays cued processionals and a mixed dance repertoire, follows the planner's timeline, handles last-minute song and volume changes, and often MCs.

Worship service music: organist, pianist, cantor, choir accompanist, or praise-band member plays hymns, anthems and service music in a church or synagogue sanctuary, accompanying congregation and choir, following the clergy's pacing and adjusting length and key on the fly.

Educational presentation or recital: school assembly, children's concert, lecture-recital, senior-center or library program, in a gym, auditorium, classroom or community room; the musician plays selected pieces, explains and demonstrates the instrument, and interacts with and answers questions from the audience.

Outdoor public performance: busking on a sidewalk or subway platform, farmers-market, street-fair or park-bandstand set; unfixed pitch, weather, ambient noise, passersby stopping and moving on, self-contained amplification and a tip jar.

tasks.label: Practice performances, individually or in rehearsal with other musicians, to master individual pieces of music or to maintain and improve skills.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Solo instrumental practice at home or a private space (bedroom, living room, home studio): a working violinist, guitarist, pianist, saxophonist or drummer warms up, drills difficult passages slowly, self-critiques tone and intonation, and works new repertoire up to performance standard on their own instrument, amid household clutter, furniture and ambient noise.

Solo vocal practice: a singer warms up the voice, works breath support, diction and range, and rehearses repertoire at home, in a church, or in a studio with a rehearsal pianist or backing track, self-monitoring pitch and tone.

Small-group rehearsal (rock/jazz/cover band, string quartet, worship team) in a rented rehearsal studio, church hall or club backroom: running charts and songs with 2-6 other players, stopping to fix arrangements, matching tempo, feel and dynamics, taking verbal direction from the bandleader.

Large-ensemble rehearsal (orchestra, big band, chorus, musical-theatre pit) in a rehearsal hall or school music room under a conductor: reading a written part, following the baton, and responding to spoken instructions such as 'from bar 42, softer, watch the cutoff' while blending with a section.

On-site dress rehearsal or sound check at the performance venue: the group sets up on stage, runs the set through the PA and monitors, and adjusts to the room's acoustics and the sound engineer's requests in the hour before the show.

instances.label: Small-group live gig at a bar, club, brewery or restaurant: playing electric guitar, bass, drums or keyboards (often while singing) through two or three sets of covers and originals, counting off tunes, stretching or cutting arrangements, taking requests, and adjusting dynamics and feel to the room and crowd.

Concert with a large ensemble - symphony orchestra, wind band, big band or musical-theatre pit - in a concert hall or theatre: reading a notated part on a violin, wind, brass or percussion chair, following a conductor's beat and cues, tuning and blending with the section, and handling rehearsal changes.

Recording or broadcast session in a studio: playing an instrumental part to a click over multiple takes and overdubs, revising phrasing, tone and feel on the producer's verbal direction, and matching the arrangement until an acceptable take is captured.

Wedding, private party or corporate event in a banquet room, tent or private residence: performing a set list on the client's instrument or the player's own, cueing music to live event moments (processional, first dance, toasts), taking requests and adapting length on the fly.

Worship service, funeral or school ceremony: playing organ, piano or guitar to accompany a congregation, choir or soloist, leading and following live singing, transposing, and extending or shortening music to fit the flow of the service.

Solo instrumental performance of a prepared program with no live adaptation required - cocktail/lobby piano at a hotel, restaurant or museum, background or featured set at an exhibition or ticketed showcase - playing a fixed repertoire on a keyboard or mallet instrument in a controlled venue.

instances.label: Pit-orchestra instrumentalist (violin, reeds, trumpet, percussion) for a run of a musical at a regional, touring, community or school theater: reads a printed book under a conductor, plays multi-week runs of 2.5-hour shows, handles tempo changes, cuts, and doubling instruments, and adjusts live to singers who rush, drag or drop lines.

Orchestra player in an opera or ballet performance at an opera house or performing arts center: long through-composed scores, recitative and rubato that track the singers or dancers, a conductor's beat and cues, and repertoire prepared in a few rehearsals.

Musical-theatre pit keyboardist/rehearsal pianist: plays a keyboard book with vamps and 'safeties' until cued, patch/sound changes, dialogue underscore, tech rehearsals with cuts and re-orchestrations dictated on the spot, and covers for other players' errors.

Solo (or duo) accompanist for a cabaret, piano-bar or nightclub floor show: backs singers and comics, transposes to a singer's key on request, takes unrehearsed numbers and requests, plays intros, playoffs and button chords in time with stage patter.

Prepared, fixed-program accompaniment in a hall or club: a set-list revue, recital or dance recital, or silent-film screening, where the accompaniment is rehearsed, through-composed material and the performers follow the music rather than the reverse.
