Kiosks are deployed in malls, universities, retail stores and grocery chains in four states.
sources.transferJustification: Covers the 'determine visual acuity and focus (refractive error)' portion of the task only; the same article notes the kiosk cannot run medical tests such as intraocular pressure measurement.

sources.title: This AI Bot Has A Rapid View on Vision Testing - Techstrong.ai
sources.claim: The Eyebot S1 kiosk is described as a fully autonomous, AI-powered vision test taking about 90 seconds, being deployed in retail locations with Zenni Optical.

tasks.label: Prescribe, supply, fit and adjust eyeglasses, contact lenses, and other vision aids.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine adult spectacle prescription: healthy 20-55 year old with straightforward myopia/hyperopia/astigmatism seen in a clinic exam lane or retail vision center. Autorefraction and lensometry of current glasses, subjective refraction at the phoropter, prescription written and released to the optical.

Spectacle prescription requiring clinical judgment: children and teens, presbyopes needing a multifocal/progressive add refinement, binocular-vision or prism cases, high/unstable or post-surgical refractions, and non-adapt patients returning with a complaint. Trial-frame refinement, near/intermediate working-distance decisions, and negotiation of the final Rx in the exam lane.

Soft contact lens fitting or refit in the exam lane: keratometry/topography, selecting a diagnostic lens, inserting the trial lens onto the patient's eye, slit-lamp assessment of centration, movement and coverage, over-refraction, and teaching the patient insertion, removal and care.

Dispensing and adjusting eyeglasses at the optical counter: verifying the finished pair against the Rx, placing them on the patient's face, checking vertex, pantoscopic tilt and optical-center height, then heating and bending temples, adjusting nose pads and re-checking on the face until the fit is comfortable and aligned; includes troubleshooting complaints on previously dispensed pairs.

Specialty lens fitting: scleral, corneal RGP, hybrid, keratoconus, ortho-k or myopia-control lenses. Filling and applying the lens to the eye, fluorescein/OCT evaluation of clearance and edge alignment, multiple lens exchanges in one visit, parameter ordering and follow-up refinement.

Low-vision and other vision aids: demonstrating and fitting hand/stand magnifiers, spectacle-mounted or handheld telescopes, filters, prism, occlusion or bandage lenses for a visually impaired patient, setting working distance, and training the patient in use of the device.

instances.label: Embedded metallic corneal foreign body (e.g., grinding/welding spark) in an awake adult at the slit lamp in an optometry exam room: instill topical anesthetic, assess depth with fluorescein, dislodge the particle with a 25-gauge needle, spud or jeweler's forceps while the patient blinks and fixates, then confirm removal and treat the epithelial defect.

Loose superficial conjunctival or corneal surface particle (dust, sand, plant matter, mascara): sterile saline lavage or lift-off with a moistened cotton-tipped applicator at the slit lamp, followed by fluorescein check of the ocular surface.

Subtarsal foreign body causing vertical corneal abrasions: evert (and sometimes double-evert) the upper eyelid on an uncomfortable, tearing patient, sweep the tarsal conjunctiva with a swab or irrigation, and verify the lid and fornices are clear.

Metallic foreign body with residual rust ring: after particle removal, burr the rust and surrounding infiltrate away with an Alger brush under slit-lamp magnification, judging when to stop at Bowman's layer to limit scarring, especially near the visual axis.

Difficult presentation: pediatric, elderly or highly photophobic patient with blepharospasm, multiple embedded particles or dirty organic debris, requiring repeated repositioning, lid holding, extra anesthetic, and a judgment about deep/penetrating injury and referral to ophthalmology.

instances.label: Hospital central IV room / cleanroom: scheduled and batch non-hazardous admixtures from the validated formulary — antibiotic minibags, standard-concentration vasoactive and sedation drips, prefilled syringes stocked for the OR, ED and floors. Home infusion / alternate-site pharmacy cleanroom: patient-specific multi-day supplies of antibiotics or specialty infusions filled into IV minibags, syringes, pump cassettes and elastomeric pumps for administration in the patient's home, with extended beyond-use dating and patient-specific labeling.

Immediate-use preparation at or near the point of care: the ED or OR pharmacist reconstitutes and draws up drugs during a resuscitation, rapid-sequence intubation or an emergent OR case (push-dose pressors, thrombolytic, antidote), working at a bedside cart or anteroom counter in minutes.

Non-library / non-standard sterile preparations made manually in a laminar-airflow hood: investigational-trial IV drugs, unusual concentrations or diluents, neonatal micro-dilutions, intrathecal or intraocular preparations, novel containers or devices not validated on any automated system.

instances.label: Community/retail pharmacy final product verification (PV2): pharmacist confirms the tablets/capsules or manufacturer package in the filled vial are the prescribed drug, strength and dosage form (imprint, color, shape, NDC on stock bottle), and that the product looks intact and undamaged; high volume, look-alike/sound-alike risk, frequent interruptions.

Stock receiving and shelf integrity in a pharmacy stockroom: verifying that delivered product matches the invoice by drug, strength, package size, lot and expiration date; checking for damaged, degraded, recalled or suspect/illegitimate product before it goes on the shelf.

Compounding pharmacy (503A/503B or hospital batch compounding): assessing strength and purity of a compounded batch — in-process weight/volume/pH checks plus potency assay and sterility/endotoxin testing of pulled samples against specification before release.

Identification of unknown or unlabeled medications: brown-bag review, loose or mixed tablets from a patient's pillbox, home meds presented on hospital admission, or foreign/unlabeled products; pharmacist identifies drug and strength from imprint/appearance and judges whether the product is genuine and usable.

Nuclear pharmacy hot lab: batch quality control of radiopharmaceuticals before dose dispensing — radiochemical purity and identity, pH, clarity/color, residual solvents/Kryptofix, and activity assay in a dose calibrator, under tight time pressure.

Hospital/health-system central pharmacy: purchase against GPO/wholesaler contracts, receive bulk cartons at the dock, put away into the pharmacy stockroom/carousel and unit-dose bins, run cycle counts and expiration checks, and pick replenishment for automated dispensing cabinets on the units.

Controlled substances (CII-CV): place CSOS/DEA-222 orders, receive under witness, count each package into the narcotics safe or vault, and reconcile the perpetual inventory; secure storage and diversion-proof handling throughout.

Cold-chain and specialty items (vaccines, insulin, biologics): order limited quantities, receive within the temperature window, verify shipping indicators, place into a medical-grade refrigerator/freezer, log and monitor temperatures, rotate by expiry.

Non-drug medical supplies, OTC/diabetic supplies and compounding chemicals, plus shortage management: source alternates from secondary suppliers when a drug is short, then receive and shelve heterogeneous, odd-shaped goods in the stockroom.

Central-fill / mail-order / automated micro-fulfillment pharmacy: pharmacist oversees bulk drug inventory in a purpose-built automated facility - bulk stock received on pallets, inducted into automated storage, replenished into dispensing canisters, lot/expiry tracked.

instances.label: Community/retail pharmacy counter: pharmacist counsels a patient who just bought or was prescribed a home blood pressure monitor — explains cuff sizing and placement, resting/measurement technique, target ranges, how to log readings and when to contact the prescriber. Purpose is patient understanding and behavior change.

Newly diagnosed diabetes patient at the pharmacy or clinic: pharmacist trains the person to use a glucometer or continuous glucose monitor — lancing, strips/sensor, calibration, interpreting values, hypo/hyperglycemia action steps, diet and foot-care advice. Output is an educated, self-managing patient.

Opportunistic prevention counseling at the point of dispensing or via phone/telehealth: smoking-cessation advice, weight/diet/exercise counseling, adherence coaching, recommending vaccines or screenings, distributing educational leaflets. Purely informational exchange, often 2-5 minutes.

Community outreach event (health fair, senior center, employer wellness day): pharmacist staffs a booth or gives a short talk on hypertension or diabetes prevention, demonstrates device use to walk-up attendees, hands out materials, and may check a blood pressure reading as a screening hook. Variable crowd and setting.

Scheduled structured education session in a health-system, clinic, or MTM setting: pharmacist runs a diabetes self-management or hypertension education appointment/class, reviews the patient's device technique and home readings, documents the encounter in the record and sends recommendations to the prescriber.
